cue.card: Describe a person you know who works for themselves.
points: and explain whether you would like to work like them
model: I’d like to talk about my friend Quang, who has been a freelance video editor for about five years.

He works for a mix of clients — small businesses that need promotional videos, YouTubers and occasionally advertising agencies. Most of his projects come through a freelancing platform and word of mouth, and he works from a small studio he’s set up in his flat.

He started almost by accident. He was working in marketing and began editing videos for friends at weekends. When his side income started to approach his salary, he took the risk of going independent. The first year was precarious — some months he earned very little, and he had to learn to chase late payments and pay his own social insurance.

I admire his autonomy; he chooses projects he enjoys, sets his own hours and takes holidays when he wants. But I’m honestly not sure I’d want to work like him, at least not yet. He works long hours before deadlines, has no paid sick leave and admits that the uncertainty can be stressful. For me, flexibility is a mixed blessing, so I’d probably prefer a portfolio career — a stable main job plus freelance work on the side.

write.prompt: The number of people working in the gig economy, such as delivery riders and freelance workers, is increasing. Do the advantages of this trend outweigh the disadvantages?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase; position — disadvantages outweigh unless regulated
Body 1: advantages — flexibility, low barriers, consumer convenience, side income
Body 2: disadvantages — insecurity, no benefits, algorithmic control, pressure on public systems
Conclusion: regulate to keep benefits and reduce harms
model: In recent years, digital platforms have enabled a rapid expansion of the so-called gig economy, in which people are paid for individual tasks rather than holding permanent jobs. While this trend offers genuine benefits, I believe that, in its current form, its disadvantages outweigh its advantages.

Supporters of the gig economy point to its flexibility. Workers can choose when and how much they work, which suits students, parents with irregular schedules and those seeking a side income. Barriers to entry are low, so people who struggle to find conventional employment can start earning quickly. Consumers also benefit from services that are cheaper and more convenient than ever before, from food delivery to on-demand design work.

However, these advantages come at a considerable cost to workers. Because they are usually classified as self-employed, gig workers typically receive no sick pay, holiday pay or social insurance, leaving them vulnerable if they fall ill or the platform reduces its rates. Their incomes are often unpredictable, and many must work very long hours to earn a reasonable wage after commission. Moreover, they are frequently managed by algorithms and rating systems that can deactivate them with little explanation. In the long term, this creates pressure on public welfare systems, which may have to support older workers who never contributed to pensions.

In conclusion, although the gig economy provides flexibility and convenience, the insecurity it imposes on workers is a serious problem. I believe governments should regulate platforms so that gig workers receive basic protections, allowing society to retain the benefits of this model while reducing its most harmful effects.

lines.t: Are you good at saving money?
lines.vi: Bạn có giỏi tiết kiệm tiền không?

lines.t: I’ve got better. I used to spend everything before payday, but now I put fifteen percent of my salary into a savings account automatically, which builds an emergency fund without much effort.
lines.vi: Tôi đã khá hơn. Trước đây tôi tiêu hết trước ngày lương, nhưng giờ tôi tự động chuyển mười lăm phần trăm lương vào tài khoản tiết kiệm, giúp xây quỹ dự phòng mà không tốn sức.

lines.t: Who taught you about money?
lines.vi: Ai dạy bạn về tiền bạc?

lines.t: Mostly my mother — she’s very frugal and kept a notebook of every expense. School taught us almost nothing about personal finance, which I think is a real gap.
lines.vi: Chủ yếu là mẹ tôi — bà rất tằn tiện và ghi sổ mọi khoản chi. Trường học hầu như không dạy gì về tài chính cá nhân, tôi nghĩ đó là khoảng trống thật sự.

lines.t: Do you use buy now, pay later services?
lines.vi: Bạn có dùng dịch vụ mua trước trả sau không?

lines.t: I tried it once for a laptop because it was interest-free, but I avoid it now. It makes spending feel painless, and it’s easy to lose track of several instalments at once.
lines.vi: Tôi từng dùng một lần mua laptop vì không lãi, nhưng giờ tôi tránh. Nó khiến tiêu tiền không cảm thấy đau, và dễ mất kiểm soát khi trả góp nhiều khoản cùng lúc.

sents.t: Household debt in many Asian economies has grown significantly over the past decade.
sents.vi: Nợ hộ gia đình ở nhiều nền kinh tế châu Á tăng đáng kể trong thập kỷ qua.

sents.t: Much of the growth among young adults comes from credit cards, instalment plans and app-based loans.
sents.vi: Phần lớn mức tăng ở người trẻ đến từ thẻ tín dụng, trả góp và khoản vay qua ứng dụng.

sents.t: Some unlicensed lending apps charge annual interest rates of several hundred percent.
sents.vi: Một số ứng dụng cho vay không phép tính lãi suất năm lên tới vài trăm phần trăm.

sents.t: Surveys suggest that fewer than half of young adults can correctly answer basic questions about interest and inflation.
sents.vi: Khảo sát cho thấy chưa đến một nửa người trẻ trả lời đúng câu hỏi cơ bản về lãi và lạm phát.

sents.t: As a result, several governments are adding financial education to the school curriculum.
sents.vi: Kết quả là một số chính phủ đang đưa giáo dục tài chính vào chương trình học.

q.q: Some lending apps charge extremely high interest.
Most young adults understand inflation well.
Financial education has reduced debt in all countries that introduced it.

gram.title: Describing trends
gram.rule: rise / increase / grow + adverb (sharply, steadily) · a sharp rise in + noun · has risen by / to
gram.note: For Part 3 and Writing, describe trends with a verb + adverb or an adjective + noun: Debt has risen sharply. There has been a steady increase in borrowing. Use by for the size of change and to for the final level.

ex.t: Consumer debt has risen sharply in recent years.
ex.vi: Nợ tiêu dùng tăng mạnh những năm gần đây.

ex.t: There has been a steady increase in online lending.

ex.t: Interest rates have dropped to their lowest level.

lines.t: Why do young people get into debt?
lines.vi: Vì sao người trẻ mắc nợ?

lines.t: Partly social pressure — social media constantly shows people with new phones and holidays, so there’s a temptation to live beyond your means. Easy credit makes it worse, because apps approve loans in minutes without checking whether you can afford them.
lines.vi: Một phần do áp lực xã hội — mạng xã hội liên tục cho thấy người ta có điện thoại mới, đi du lịch, nên dễ bị cám dỗ tiêu quá khả năng. Tín dụng dễ dãi làm tệ hơn, vì ứng dụng duyệt vay trong vài phút mà không kiểm tra khả năng trả.

lines.t: Should schools teach financial skills?
lines.vi: Trường học có nên dạy kỹ năng tài chính không?

lines.t: Absolutely. Understanding compound interest, budgeting and scams is arguably as important as algebra for most people. If students learned these skills early, fewer would fall into debt traps.
lines.vi: Hoàn toàn nên. Hiểu lãi kép, lập ngân sách và nhận diện lừa đảo có lẽ quan trọng như đại số với hầu hết mọi người. Nếu học sinh học sớm, sẽ ít người rơi vào bẫy nợ hơn.

lines.t: Is borrowing money always bad?
lines.vi: Vay tiền có luôn xấu không?

lines.t: No, borrowing to invest in education or a home can be sensible. The problem is borrowing at high interest for things that lose value quickly, like gadgets or fashion.
lines.vi: Không, vay để đầu tư vào học tập hay nhà ở có thể hợp lý. Vấn đề là vay lãi cao cho những thứ mất giá nhanh như thiết bị hay thời trang.

gram2.title: Arguably, it could be argued that…
gram2.rule: arguably + adjective / clause · It could be argued that … · One could argue that …
gram2.note: These phrases present a strong opinion in a measured way, which examiners reward: Financial literacy is arguably more useful than algebra. It could be argued that apps are designed to encourage debt.

ex.t: Financial literacy is arguably as important as reading.
ex.vi: Hiểu biết tài chính có lẽ quan trọng như đọc viết.

ex.t: It could be argued that easy credit harms the poor most.
ex.vi: Có thể cho rằng tín dụng dễ dãi gây hại nhất cho người nghèo.

ex.t: One could argue that debt is a choice.
ex.vi: Người ta có thể cho rằng nợ là một lựa chọn.

ex.t: This is arguably the biggest risk for students.
ex.vi: Đây có lẽ là rủi ro lớn nhất với sinh viên.

drill.t: It could be ___ that banks lend too easily.
drill.vi: Có thể cho rằng ngân hàng cho vay quá dễ.

drill.t: Saving early is ___ the best financial habit.
drill.vi: Tiết kiệm sớm có lẽ là thói quen tài chính tốt nhất.

drill.t: One ___ argue that apps target the young.
drill.vi: Có thể cho rằng ứng dụng nhắm vào người trẻ.

drill.t: It ___ be argued that inflation hurts savers.
drill.vi: Có thể cho rằng lạm phát gây hại cho người tiết kiệm.

cue.card: Describe a time when you saved money for something special.
points: and explain how you felt when you finally bought it
model: I’d like to talk about the year I spent saving for my first trip abroad — two weeks backpacking in Japan, when I was twenty-four.
It took me about fourteen months. At the time I was on a fairly modest salary, and Japan is expensive, so I needed roughly sixty million dong for flights, accommodation and a rail pass.

I set up a separate savings account and transferred a fixed amount on payday, before I could spend it. I also made some changes that were more painful than I expected: I cooked lunch instead of eating out, cancelled two streaming subscriptions and stopped buying clothes almost entirely. I tracked every expense in an app, which made me realise how much I’d been spending on small things like bubble tea — it added up to nearly a million a month.

When I finally booked the tickets, I felt an enormous sense of achievement — partly because of the trip itself, but also because it proved to me that I could be disciplined with money. The experience changed my habits permanently; I still automatically save a portion of my salary, and I’m much more sceptical of instalment plans and impulse purchases. The trip was wonderful, but arguably the lesson was even more valuable.

write.prompt: Many young people today have significant debts from credit cards and personal loans. What are the causes of this problem, and what measures could be taken to solve it?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase; preview causes and measures
Body 1: causes — easy credit and apps, social pressure and consumerism, low financial literacy, high living costs
Body 2: measures — regulation of lenders, financial education, employer and bank tools
Conclusion: combine regulation and education
model: In many countries, a growing number of young adults are burdened with debts from credit cards, instalment plans and personal loans. This essay will examine the main causes of this trend and suggest several measures to address it.

One major cause is the unprecedented ease of borrowing. Credit cards are offered to students, “buy now, pay later” options appear at every online checkout, and lending apps approve loans within minutes, often without proper checks on affordability. At the same time, young people are exposed to intense consumer pressure, particularly through social media, where influencers promote expensive lifestyles and products. Many also lack basic financial literacy; without understanding how interest compounds, they underestimate the true cost of borrowing. Finally, in large cities, high rents and living costs mean that some young people borrow simply to cover essential expenses.

Tackling the problem requires action from several parties. Governments should regulate lenders more strictly, capping interest rates, requiring affordability checks and shutting down unlicensed apps that charge exorbitant fees. Financial education should become a compulsory part of the school curriculum, covering budgeting, interest, inflation and common scams, so that young people enter adulthood with practical knowledge. Banks and employers can also help by offering tools that make saving automatic and by providing clear warnings when customers are approaching unsustainable levels of debt.

In conclusion, youth debt is driven by easy credit, consumer culture, low financial literacy and high living costs. A combination of stronger regulation and better education offers the most promising way to ensure that borrowing becomes a useful tool rather than a trap.

units.title: Public spaces & community life
units.goal: Discuss parks, libraries and public spaces and their role in community life, using the language of purpose and recommendation.

words.ex: Cities need more public spaces.

lines.t: Is there a park near where you live?
lines.vi: Gần nơi bạn sống có công viên không?

lines.t: Yes, a small one around a lake about ten minutes away. It’s busy from five in the morning, with older people doing tai chi and using the outdoor gym.
lines.vi: Có, một công viên nhỏ quanh hồ cách khoảng mười phút. Từ năm giờ sáng đã đông, người lớn tuổi tập dưỡng sinh và dùng dụng cụ tập ngoài trời.

lines.t: Do you often go to public libraries?
lines.vi: Bạn có hay đến thư viện công cộng không?

lines.t: Not as often as I’d like. The main city library is a bit far, but I go now and then to work quietly, because it’s free and has good air conditioning.
lines.vi: Không thường như tôi muốn. Thư viện chính của thành phố hơi xa, nhưng thỉnh thoảng tôi đến để làm việc yên tĩnh, vì miễn phí và điều hoà tốt.

lines.t: What public place would you like to see in your city?
lines.vi: Bạn muốn thành phố có thêm không gian công cộng nào?

lines.t: More playgrounds, honestly. In my district, children play in car parks because there simply isn’t anywhere else.
lines.vi: Thật lòng là thêm sân chơi. Ở quận tôi, trẻ con chơi ở bãi đỗ xe vì đơn giản là không có chỗ nào khác.

sents.t: When Hanoi turned the streets around Hoan Kiem Lake into a weekend pedestrian zone in 2016, many shop owners feared they would lose customers.
sents.vi: Khi Hà Nội biến các tuyến phố quanh hồ Hoàn Kiếm thành phố đi bộ cuối tuần năm 2016, nhiều chủ cửa hàng lo mất khách.

sents.t: Instead, footfall increased dramatically, and the area became a popular venue for families, street performers and tourists.
sents.vi: Thay vào đó, lượng người qua lại tăng mạnh, và khu vực trở thành nơi được ưa chuộng của gia đình, nghệ sĩ đường phố và du khách.

sents.t: Similar schemes have since been introduced in other cities.
sents.vi: Các mô hình tương tự đã được áp dụng ở nhiều thành phố khác.

sents.t: Urban planners say such projects show how public space can strengthen social cohesion.
sents.vi: Các nhà quy hoạch nói những dự án như vậy cho thấy không gian công cộng có thể tăng gắn kết xã hội.

sents.t: However, some residents complain about noise and rubbish on busy evenings.
sents.vi: Tuy nhiên, một số cư dân phàn nàn về tiếng ồn và rác vào những buổi tối đông người.

q.q: Shop owners initially welcomed the pedestrian zone.
Footfall around the lake increased after the change.
The pedestrian zone operates every day of the week.

gram.title: Expressing purpose: to, in order to, so as to, so that
gram.rule: to / in order to / so as to + verb · so that + subject + can / will
gram.note: Use to or in order to + verb for purpose; so as not to for negative purpose; so that + clause when the subject changes: The street was closed so that children could play safely.

ex.t: The city built parks in order to reduce heat.
ex.vi: Thành phố xây công viên để giảm nhiệt.

ex.t: Lights were installed so that people feel safe at night.
ex.vi: Đèn được lắp để mọi người thấy an toàn ban đêm.

ex.t: Cars were banned so as to reduce noise.
ex.vi: Ô tô bị cấm để giảm tiếng ồn.

ex.t: We should design spaces so that everyone can use them.
ex.vi: Nên thiết kế không gian sao cho ai cũng dùng được.

lines.t: Why are public spaces important in cities?
lines.vi: Vì sao không gian công cộng quan trọng ở thành phố?

lines.t: Because they’re among the few places where people of different backgrounds meet without paying. In crowded cities where many live in small flats, parks and squares effectively become people’s living rooms, which is vital for social cohesion.
lines.vi: Vì đó là số ít nơi người thuộc nhiều tầng lớp gặp nhau mà không phải trả tiền. Ở thành phố đông đúc nơi nhiều người sống trong căn hộ nhỏ, công viên và quảng trường thực chất là phòng khách của họ, điều thiết yếu cho gắn kết xã hội.

lines.t: Should public land be sold to developers?
lines.vi: Có nên bán đất công cho nhà đầu tư không?

lines.t: Generally not. Selling land brings short-term revenue, but once a park becomes a shopping mall it’s almost impossible to get it back. Privatisation also tends to exclude people who can’t afford to spend money.
lines.vi: Nhìn chung là không. Bán đất mang lại nguồn thu ngắn hạn, nhưng khi công viên thành trung tâm thương mại thì gần như không thể lấy lại. Tư nhân hoá cũng thường loại trừ những người không có khả năng chi tiêu.

lines.t: Who should pay for maintaining public spaces?
lines.vi: Ai nên chi trả bảo trì không gian công cộng?

lines.t: Mainly local government through taxes, but residents can share responsibility. When communities help design and look after a space, they develop a sense of ownership, and vandalism usually decreases.
lines.vi: Chủ yếu là chính quyền địa phương qua thuế, nhưng cư dân có thể chia sẻ trách nhiệm. Khi cộng đồng giúp thiết kế và chăm sóc một không gian, họ có cảm giác làm chủ và nạn phá hoại thường giảm.

gram2.title: Recommendations: It is essential that…, should, ought to, it would be advisable to
gram2.rule: It is essential / vital that + subject + (should) verb · It would be advisable to + verb
gram2.note: Formal recommendations are useful in Writing Task 2 conclusions. After It is essential that, British English often uses should; the base verb is also correct: It is essential that cities (should) protect green spaces.

ex.t: It is essential that every district has a playground.
ex.vi: Điều thiết yếu là mỗi quận đều có sân chơi.

ex.t: It would be advisable to involve residents in design.
ex.vi: Nên để cư dân tham gia thiết kế.

ex.t: Authorities ought to prevent encroachment on pavements.
ex.vi: Chính quyền nên ngăn lấn chiếm vỉa hè.

ex.t: It is vital that libraries remain free.
ex.vi: Điều thiết yếu là thư viện vẫn miễn phí.

cue.card: Describe a public place in your city that you enjoy visiting.
points: and explain why you enjoy it
model: I’d like to describe the pedestrian zone around Hoan Kiem Lake in Hanoi, which is closed to traffic every weekend from Friday evening.

It’s right in the heart of the old city. On weekend evenings the roads that are normally jammed with motorbikes become a huge open-air living room. You see families walking with small children, teenagers playing traditional games like tug of war, street musicians, people dancing and couples taking photos by the lake.
I go there most Saturday evenings, sometimes with friends and sometimes alone, just to walk and people-watch. In the hot season I usually go later, after nine, when it’s cooler but still lively.

I enjoy it for a few reasons. Most obviously, it’s a rare chance to be in the city centre without noise and exhaust fumes. But what I appreciate more is the mix of people — older residents, migrants from other provinces, foreign tourists — all sharing the same space without anyone having to pay. Hanoi is very crowded and many people live in tiny flats, so I think spaces like this are essential for social cohesion. It’s also a reminder that cities can be designed for people rather than just for vehicles.

write.prompt: In many cities, public spaces such as parks and squares are being replaced by private developments. What problems does this cause, and what can be done to protect public spaces?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase; preview problems and solutions
Body 1: problems — health and heat, social inequality and exclusion, loss of community and identity
Body 2: solutions — legal protection, planning requirements, community involvement and funding
Conclusion: public space as essential infrastructure
model: As cities expand and land becomes increasingly valuable, many parks, squares and other public spaces are being sold to private developers. This essay will discuss the problems caused by this trend and suggest ways in which public spaces can be protected.

The loss of public space has serious consequences for urban residents. Firstly, it harms public health: parks provide space for exercise, reduce air pollution and lower temperatures in increasingly hot cities, so their disappearance contributes to physical and mental health problems. Secondly, it increases social inequality. Wealthier citizens can afford private gyms, cafés and gardens, but for low-income families living in small flats, free public spaces may be the only place where children can play and adults can relax. Finally, when shared spaces are replaced by shopping centres, cities lose places where people of different backgrounds naturally meet, weakening social cohesion and local identity.

Several measures could help to protect public spaces. Governments should give parks and squares strong legal protection, making it difficult to sell or rezone them for commercial use. Urban planning regulations could also require developers to include accessible public areas, such as small parks or pedestrian streets, in every large project. In addition, involving residents in the design and care of public spaces, through consultations and community gardening schemes, creates a sense of ownership that makes these places more valued and better maintained. Adequate public funding is, of course, essential to keep them safe and attractive.

In conclusion, replacing public spaces with private developments damages health, increases inequality and weakens communities. Cities should treat public spaces not as unused land waiting for investment, but as essential infrastructure that deserves the same protection as roads and schools.

gram.title: Generalising: tend to, on the whole, by and large, the majority of
gram.rule: tend to + verb · On the whole, … · By and large, … · The majority of + plural noun
gram.note: Generalisations make Part 3 answers sound mature, but avoid absolute words like “everyone” or “always”. Use tend to and the majority of: The majority of gym members are under forty. By and large, people are more active now.

lines.vi: Tôi nghĩ trả tiền cảm giác như một cam kết, nên cho người ta cảm giác tiến bộ trước cả khi làm gì. Rồi cuộc sống thực — giờ làm dài, việc gia đình — cản trở, và động lực phai nhạt.

lines.t: Invest in grassroots sport and infrastructure — safe cycle lanes, outdoor gyms, sports fields in schools that the community can use at weekends. Making activity part of daily life works better than campaigns.

cue.card: Describe a sport or exercise you started recently.
points: and explain how you feel about it
model: I’d like to talk about pickleball, which I took up about six months ago and which has quite quickly become the highlight of my week.

For anyone who hasn’t seen it, it’s a bit like a mixture of tennis, badminton and table tennis, played with solid paddles and a plastic ball with holes on a small court. I started because a group of colleagues were playing after work and kept inviting me, and, frankly, I’d become very sedentary — my fitness tracker was showing fewer than three thousand steps on most days.

I learned mostly by playing. The basic rules are simple, so within an hour I could join a game. The more I played, the more I wanted to improve, so I watched some tutorial videos and joined a beginners’ session on Saturday mornings where a coach explained strategy, like when to stay back and when to move to the net.

I really enjoy it, mainly because it’s so social. Unlike running alone, you’re constantly chatting and laughing with your partner and opponents, and it’s not nearly as hard on your joints as football. I’ve definitely become fitter, but just as importantly I’ve made new friends outside work, which I hadn’t expected. My only worry is that it’s become something of a fitness craze, and courts are getting harder to book.

write.prompt: Although more people are aware of the importance of exercise, levels of physical activity are falling in many countries. Why is this? What can be done to encourage people to be more active?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase paradox; preview causes and solutions
Body 1: causes — sedentary jobs and long hours, urban design and car use, screens, cost/commercialisation
Body 2: solutions — active transport infrastructure, workplace and school initiatives, affordable community facilities
Conclusion: make activity the easy default
model: Paradoxically, at a time when awareness of the benefits of exercise has never been higher, many populations are becoming less physically active. This essay will explore the reasons behind this contradiction and propose measures to encourage more active lifestyles.

The main reason is that modern life has engineered physical activity out of daily routines. A growing proportion of jobs are sedentary, and long working hours and commutes leave little time or energy for exercise. Many cities are designed around cars and motorbikes, with few safe pavements or cycle lanes, so even short journeys are made by vehicle. In leisure time, screens compete successfully for people’s attention. Furthermore, the commercialisation of fitness has made exercise seem to require expensive gym memberships, equipment and supplements, discouraging those with limited budgets.

Addressing this problem requires making activity the easy option rather than an additional effort. Governments could invest in infrastructure for walking and cycling, such as safe cycle lanes and pedestrian-friendly streets, so that active travel becomes part of everyday life. Employers can contribute by offering flexible hours, standing desks and incentives for cycling to work. Schools should protect physical education and open their sports facilities to local communities at weekends. Finally, affordable or free community facilities, such as outdoor gyms and public sports courts, can make exercise accessible regardless of income.

In conclusion, falling activity levels are less a matter of ignorance than of environments and lifestyles that discourage movement. By redesigning cities, workplaces and public facilities so that being active is convenient and affordable, societies can turn awareness into action.

lines.t: Do you follow news about medical science?
lines.vi: Bạn có theo dõi tin về y học không?

lines.t: Fairly closely, partly because my sister is a nurse. I’m particularly interested in gene therapies, since some conditions that were untreatable when I was a child can now be managed.
lines.vi: Khá sát, một phần vì chị tôi là điều dưỡng. Tôi đặc biệt quan tâm đến liệu pháp gen, vì một số bệnh không chữa được hồi tôi còn nhỏ giờ đã kiểm soát được.

lines.t: Would you eat genetically modified food?
lines.vi: Bạn có ăn thực phẩm biến đổi gen không?

lines.t: I probably already do without knowing it. As long as it’s been properly tested, I don’t have a problem with it; what concerns me more is how much pesticide is used on ordinary crops.
lines.vi: Có lẽ tôi đã ăn mà không biết. Miễn là nó được kiểm nghiệm đúng cách, tôi không có vấn đề gì; điều tôi lo hơn là lượng thuốc trừ sâu dùng cho cây trồng thông thường.

lines.t: Would you take a DNA test to learn about your ancestry?
lines.vi: Bạn có làm xét nghiệm ADN để tìm hiểu tổ tiên không?

lines.t: I’m tempted, but I’d want to know exactly who could access the data. Genetic information is shared with your relatives, so it isn’t only your privacy at stake.
lines.vi: Tôi cũng muốn, nhưng tôi cần biết chính xác ai có thể truy cập dữ liệu. Thông tin gen chia sẻ với họ hàng của bạn, nên không chỉ quyền riêng tư của riêng bạn bị ảnh hưởng.

sents.t: In 2018, a researcher in China announced that he had edited the genes of twin girls before birth, aiming to make them resistant to HIV.
sents.vi: Năm 2018, một nhà nghiên cứu ở Trung Quốc tuyên bố đã chỉnh gen của cặp song sinh nữ trước khi sinh, nhằm giúp họ kháng HIV.

sents.t: The announcement was condemned almost universally by scientists, who argued that the risks were unknown and the medical need was minimal.
sents.vi: Thông báo bị giới khoa học gần như đồng loạt lên án, vì rủi ro chưa được biết và nhu cầu y tế rất nhỏ.

sents.t: Because the changes were made to embryos, they could be passed on to future generations.
sents.vi: Vì thay đổi được thực hiện trên phôi, chúng có thể truyền sang thế hệ sau.

sents.t: The researcher was later sentenced to three years in prison for illegal medical practice.
sents.vi: Nhà nghiên cứu sau đó bị kết án ba năm tù vì hành nghề y trái phép.

sents.t: The case prompted calls for a global agreement on which uses of gene editing should be permitted.
sents.vi: Vụ việc dẫn đến lời kêu gọi một thoả thuận toàn cầu về những ứng dụng chỉnh sửa gen nên được cho phép.

q.q: Most scientists supported the researcher’s experiment.
The genetic changes could be inherited by the twins’ children.
A global agreement on gene editing was signed in 2020.

gram.title: Conditionals without “if”
gram.rule: provided / providing that · as long as · on condition that · unless · otherwise · supposing · but for + noun
gram.note: Varying how you express conditions is a quick way to show grammatical range. Provided that and as long as introduce a necessary condition. Unless means “if … not”. Otherwise follows a sentence: Regulation is essential; otherwise, abuses will occur. But for + noun is formal: But for vaccines, millions more would have died.

ex.t: Gene therapy is acceptable provided that it treats serious illness.
ex.vi: Liệu pháp gen chấp nhận được với điều kiện nó điều trị bệnh nặng.

ex.t: Unless research is regulated, accidents are inevitable.
ex.vi: Nếu nghiên cứu không được quản lý, tai nạn là không tránh khỏi.

ex.t: Data must be protected; otherwise, people will refuse testing.
ex.vi: Dữ liệu phải được bảo vệ; nếu không, người ta sẽ từ chối xét nghiệm.

ex.t: But for antibiotics, many of us would not be alive.

lines.t: Should there be limits on genetic research?
lines.vi: Có nên giới hạn nghiên cứu gen không?

lines.t: Absolutely, though the limits should be about applications rather than knowledge itself. Editing genes in an adult to cure a disease affects only that person, provided they consent. Editing embryos is different, because the changes are inherited and future generations can’t consent at all.
lines.vi: Chắc chắn, dù giới hạn nên áp lên ứng dụng chứ không phải bản thân tri thức. Chỉnh gen ở người trưởng thành để chữa bệnh chỉ ảnh hưởng người đó, miễn là họ đồng ý. Chỉnh phôi thì khác, vì thay đổi được di truyền và thế hệ sau hoàn toàn không thể đồng ý.

lines.t: Could gene editing make society more unequal?
lines.vi: Chỉnh sửa gen có thể làm xã hội bất bình đẳng hơn?

lines.t: That’s probably my biggest concern. The first treatments cost over a million dollars per patient, so unless governments subsidise them, wealthy families could buy health advantages that others can’t — and in the worst case, pass them on to their children.
lines.vi: Đó có lẽ là mối lo lớn nhất của tôi. Những liệu pháp đầu tiên tốn hơn một triệu đô la mỗi bệnh nhân, nên trừ khi chính phủ trợ giá, các gia đình giàu có thể mua lợi thế sức khoẻ mà người khác không mua được — và tệ nhất là truyền lại cho con cái.

lines.t: Who should decide what is ethical: scientists or the public?
lines.vi: Ai nên quyết định điều gì là đạo đức: nhà khoa học hay công chúng?

lines.t: Both, but neither alone. Scientists understand the risks, yet they also have an interest in continuing their work. The public brings different values. Independent ethics committees that include non-scientists seem like the most balanced solution.
lines.vi: Cả hai, nhưng không bên nào riêng lẻ. Nhà khoa học hiểu rủi ro, nhưng họ cũng có lợi ích trong việc tiếp tục công việc. Công chúng mang đến những giá trị khác. Các hội đồng đạo đức độc lập có cả người ngoài ngành có vẻ là giải pháp cân bằng nhất.

gram2.title: Language for evidence and its limits
gram2.rule: Research suggests / indicates that … · There is (little / growing / mixed) evidence that … · The evidence is inconclusive. · This is not to say that …
gram2.note: High-band essays distinguish between what is proven, likely and uncertain. Suggest and indicate are more cautious than show or prove. Use growing evidence for an emerging consensus and mixed or inconclusive for genuine uncertainty. This is not to say that … prevents your reader from over-interpreting your point.

cue.card: Describe a scientific development that you think has had a big impact.
points: and explain why you think its impact is so significant
model: I’d like to talk about mRNA vaccines, which most people first heard of in late 2020, when they became the first COVID-19 vaccines approved in many countries.

Although they seemed to appear overnight, the technology had actually been developed slowly over about thirty years, often with very little funding. The basic idea is that instead of injecting a weakened virus, you give the body a set of instructions for making one harmless protein from the virus, so the immune system learns to recognise it. Because those instructions can be rewritten quickly, a new vaccine can be designed in days rather than years.

Its impact has been enormous. Within a year, hundreds of millions of doses had been given, and studies estimate that the vaccines prevented millions of deaths. But what I find most significant is the potential beyond COVID: trials are now under way for cancer vaccines tailored to individual patients. Provided those trials succeed, it could change treatment for some of the most common causes of death. It’s also a powerful reminder that basic research which looks unpromising for decades can suddenly become essential — which is a strong argument for funding science even when the benefits aren’t obvious.

write.prompt: Scientists can now alter the genes of humans, plants and animals. Some people believe this should be encouraged, while others think it is dangerous. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
plan: Introduction: paraphrase + nuanced position (encourage for crops and somatic therapy; strict limits on heritable human editing)
Body 1: case for — disease, food security, evidence of safety for GM crops
Body 2: case against — unforeseen consequences, heritable changes and consent, inequality, slippery slope
Conclusion: support with distinctions and governance
model: Advances in genetic science now allow researchers to modify the DNA of crops, livestock and even human beings. While some regard these techniques as a breakthrough that should be actively promoted, others consider them a threat. In my view, genetic modification should be encouraged in agriculture and in treating disease in individual patients, but altering human embryos should remain strictly prohibited for the time being.

The potential benefits are considerable. Gene therapies have already enabled some children with previously fatal inherited conditions to live relatively normal lives, and similar techniques are being tested against certain cancers. In agriculture, crops engineered to tolerate drought or resist pests could help feed a growing population as climate change reduces yields in many regions. Moreover, decades of research and several major scientific reviews have found no evidence that approved genetically modified foods are less safe to eat than conventional ones.

Nevertheless, opponents raise legitimate concerns. Genes interact in complex ways, so modifications may have unforeseen consequences that only become apparent years later. This risk is especially serious when changes are made to embryos, since they are passed on to future generations, none of whom can give consent. There is also an issue of fairness: early gene therapies cost hundreds of thousands of dollars, and unless access is regulated, they could allow wealthy families to purchase biological advantages, creating a slippery slope towards so-called designer babies.

In conclusion, I believe the dangers of genetic technology do not justify rejecting it altogether, as its capacity to cure disease and strengthen food security is too valuable. However, these benefits can only be realised safely provided that research is subject to independent oversight, treatments are made affordable, and heritable changes to the human genome remain off-limits until there is a broad international consensus.

units.title: Economic inequality

lines.t: Is it easy for young people to save money?
lines.vi: Người trẻ tiết kiệm tiền có dễ không?

lines.t: Much harder than it was for my parents, mainly because rent takes such a large share of a starting salary. Most of my friends save something, but nowhere near enough to buy a home.
lines.vi: Khó hơn nhiều so với thời bố mẹ tôi, chủ yếu vì tiền thuê nhà chiếm phần lớn lương khởi điểm. Phần lớn bạn tôi có tiết kiệm, nhưng còn xa mới đủ mua nhà.

lines.t: Did your family teach you about money?
lines.vi: Gia đình có dạy bạn về tiền bạc không?

lines.t: In a practical way, yes. My mother ran a small shop, so I learned early that income and profit aren’t the same thing, and that you should always have a safety net.
lines.vi: Theo cách thực tế thì có. Mẹ tôi mở một cửa hàng nhỏ, nên tôi sớm học được rằng doanh thu và lợi nhuận không giống nhau, và luôn phải có quỹ dự phòng.

lines.t: Would you like to be very rich?
lines.vi: Bạn có muốn rất giàu không?

lines.t: Comfortable, yes; very rich, not particularly. Beyond a certain point, I suspect extra money brings more worries than happiness.
lines.vi: Đủ thoải mái thì có; rất giàu thì không hẳn. Vượt quá một mức nào đó, tôi đoán thêm tiền mang lại nhiều lo lắng hơn hạnh phúc.

sents.t: In Denmark, it would take an estimated two generations for a family at the bottom to reach average income.
sents.vi: Ở Đan Mạch, ước tính cần hai thế hệ để một gia đình ở đáy đạt thu nhập trung bình.

sents.vi: Ở một số nước Mỹ Latinh, hành trình tương tự cần chín thế hệ trở lên.

sents.t: Countries with higher mobility tend to invest heavily in early childhood education and healthcare.
sents.vi: Các nước có mức dịch chuyển cao hơn thường đầu tư mạnh vào giáo dục mầm non và y tế.

sents.t: This suggests that inequality of opportunity, not just of income, is shaped by policy choices.
sents.vi: Điều này cho thấy bất bình đẳng về cơ hội, không chỉ về thu nhập, được định hình bởi lựa chọn chính sách.

Countries with high mobility spend little on early education.

gram.title: Precise comparison
gram.rule: marginally / slightly / considerably / substantially / significantly + comparative · nowhere near as … as · not nearly as … as · just as … as · twice / three times as … as
gram.note: At band 7+, examiners look for comparisons that state how big a difference is. Choose the adverb that matches the data: marginally for tiny differences, substantially for large ones. Nowhere near as … as and not nearly as … as are strong negative comparisons common in speech and writing.

ex.t: Incomes in the capital are substantially higher than in rural areas.
ex.vi: Thu nhập ở thủ đô cao hơn đáng kể so với nông thôn.

ex.t: The gap narrowed only marginally after the reform.
ex.vi: Khoảng cách chỉ thu hẹp không đáng kể sau cải cách.

ex.t: Wages are nowhere near as high as house prices suggest they should be.
ex.vi: Lương còn xa mới cao như giá nhà ngụ ý.

ex.t: Women earn almost as much as men in this sector.
ex.vi: Phụ nữ kiếm gần bằng nam giới trong ngành này.

drill.vi: Nhóm 10% giàu nhất kiếm gấp bốn lần nửa dưới.

lines.t: Is some inequality necessary in society?
lines.vi: Một mức bất bình đẳng có cần thiết cho xã hội không?

lines.t: Some, probably. If everyone earned exactly the same regardless of effort or skill, there’d be little incentive to train as a surgeon or start a risky business. The problem arises when inequality becomes entrenched — when outcomes depend more on which family you were born into than on what you do.
lines.vi: Có lẽ là một chút. Nếu ai cũng kiếm y như nhau bất kể nỗ lực hay kỹ năng, sẽ ít động lực để học làm bác sĩ phẫu thuật hay mở một doanh nghiệp rủi ro. Vấn đề nảy sinh khi bất bình đẳng trở nên cố hữu — khi kết quả phụ thuộc vào gia đình bạn sinh ra hơn là việc bạn làm.

lines.t: Do rich people have a responsibility to help the poor?
lines.vi: Người giàu có trách nhiệm giúp người nghèo không?

lines.t: I’d say their main responsibility is simply to pay their fair share of tax. Charity is admirable, but it’s voluntary and unpredictable; a fair tax system with no loopholes does far more to fund schools and hospitals.
lines.vi: Tôi cho rằng trách nhiệm chính của họ đơn giản là đóng đủ phần thuế công bằng. Từ thiện đáng ngưỡng mộ, nhưng mang tính tự nguyện và khó lường; một hệ thống thuế công bằng không kẽ hở làm được nhiều hơn để tài trợ trường học và bệnh viện.

lines.t: Does economic growth automatically reduce poverty?
lines.vi: Tăng trưởng kinh tế có tự động giảm nghèo không?

lines.t: It helps enormously, as East Asia shows. But it doesn’t automatically trickle down. Where growth is concentrated in a few sectors or regions, large groups can be left behind, so you need deliberate policies — rural roads, education, a basic safety net — to spread the benefits.
lines.vi: Nó giúp rất nhiều, như Đông Á cho thấy. Nhưng nó không tự động thẩm thấu xuống. Khi tăng trưởng tập trung vào vài ngành hay vùng, nhiều nhóm lớn có thể bị bỏ lại, nên cần chính sách có chủ đích — đường nông thôn, giáo dục, lưới an sinh cơ bản — để lan toả lợi ích.

gram2.title: Collocations for economic change
gram2.rule: widen / narrow / bridge / close the gap · a growing / persistent / stark disparity · bear the brunt of · fall behind · lift people out of poverty
gram2.note: Lexical Resource at band 7+ depends on natural collocations, not rare single words. Learn verbs and adjectives that typically go with key nouns: the gap widens or narrows; disparities are stark or persistent; groups bear the brunt of a crisis. Using these chunks makes writing sound fluent and precise.

cue.card: Describe a person you know who has worked hard to improve their life.
points: what their situation was like before
what they did to change it
and explain what you have learned from them
model: I’d like to talk about my cousin Hoa, who is now an accountant at an international firm in Ho Chi Minh City, which is remarkable given where she started.

She grew up in a farming village in Nghe An, one of the poorer provinces, and her parents left school at fourteen. When she was in secondary school, her father was injured and couldn’t work for two years, so she spent her evenings helping on the farm instead of studying. Nobody in her family had ever been to university, and honestly, most people expected her to work in a factory.

What changed things was a combination of her own determination and a bit of support at the right moment. A teacher noticed she was exceptionally good at maths and gave her extra lessons for free, and she won a scholarship that covered her tuition fees. At university she worked part-time in a café and taught herself English from free online resources. What I’ve learned from her is twofold. First, obviously, persistence matters. But second — and she always insists on this — talent alone isn’t enough. But for that teacher and the scholarship, she says she would almost certainly have fallen behind, which is why I think opportunities for young people like her shouldn’t depend on luck.

write.prompt: The table below shows the share of national income received by the top 10% and the bottom 50% of the population in four countries in 1980 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
write.data:
Country     Top 10% (1980)   Top 10% (2020)   Bottom 50% (1980)   Bottom 50% (2020)
Country A   34%              47%              20%                 13%
Country B   31%              33%              23%                 22%
Country C   45%              41%              12%                 15%
Country D   28%              29%              25%                 24%
plan: Introduction: paraphrase
Overview: A became far more unequal; C was the only one where inequality fell; B and D stayed stable and most equal
Body 1: Country A and C — opposite directions, with figures
Body 2: B and D — marginal change; comparison of 2020 levels
model: The table compares the proportion of national income earned by the richest tenth and the poorest half of the population in four countries in 1980 and 2020.

Overall, the top 10% received a substantially larger share of income than the bottom 50% in every country and in both years. Inequality rose sharply in Country A, whereas Country C was the only nation where the gap narrowed. Countries B and D changed only marginally and remained the most equal.

Country A experienced by far the most dramatic shift. The share of income going to its top earners climbed from just over a third (34%) to almost half (47%), while the share received by the poorest half shrank from a fifth to 13%. Country C moved in the opposite direction: although it began as the most unequal country, with the top tenth earning 45% and the bottom half only 12%, these figures converged slightly to 41% and 15% respectively by 2020.

By contrast, the distribution in Countries B and D was relatively stable. In both, the top 10% gained only one or two percentage points, and the share of the bottom 50% fell by just one point. Country D remained the most equal throughout, with its poorest half receiving almost as much income as its richest tenth in 2020 (24% compared with 29%).

lines.t: Would you like to live in another country?
lines.vi: Bạn có muốn sống ở nước khác không?

lines.t: For a few years, yes — ideally somewhere I could gain experience in my field. Much as I’d enjoy the adventure, I can’t imagine settling permanently away from my family.
lines.vi: Vài năm thì có — lý tưởng là nơi tôi tích luỹ được kinh nghiệm chuyên môn. Dù rất muốn trải nghiệm, tôi không hình dung nổi việc định cư lâu dài xa gia đình.

lines.t: Do you know anyone who lives abroad?
lines.vi: Bạn có quen ai sống ở nước ngoài không?

lines.t: Quite a few people. My uncle has lived in Germany since the 1980s, and two university friends work in Japan. They all say the first winter is the hardest — that’s when people get really homesick.
lines.vi: Khá nhiều người. Chú tôi sống ở Đức từ những năm 1980, và hai bạn đại học làm việc ở Nhật. Họ đều nói mùa đông đầu tiên khó nhất — đó là lúc người ta nhớ nhà thật sự.

lines.t: What would you miss most if you moved abroad?
lines.vi: Bạn sẽ nhớ gì nhất nếu chuyển ra nước ngoài?

lines.t: Honestly, the food, and the noise. It sounds strange, but when I travel to quiet cities, the silence at night makes me feel oddly lonely.
lines.vi: Thật lòng là đồ ăn, và sự ồn ào. Nghe lạ, nhưng khi đến những thành phố yên tĩnh, sự im lặng ban đêm khiến tôi cô đơn một cách kỳ lạ.

sents.t: The Philippines trains far more nurses than its own hospitals employ, partly because many plan to work abroad.
sents.vi: Philippines đào tạo nhiều điều dưỡng hơn hẳn số bệnh viện trong nước tuyển dụng, một phần vì nhiều người dự định làm việc ở nước ngoài.

sents.t: Critics argue that this leaves rural clinics understaffed.
sents.vi: Những người phản đối cho rằng điều này khiến các phòng khám nông thôn thiếu nhân lực.

sents.t: However, the prospect of emigration also persuades more young people to study nursing in the first place.
sents.vi: Tuy nhiên, triển vọng di cư cũng thuyết phục nhiều người trẻ học điều dưỡng ngay từ đầu.

sents.t: Some of these graduates stay at home, so the country may end up with more nurses than it would otherwise have had.
sents.vi: Một số người tốt nghiệp ở lại trong nước, nên quốc gia có thể có nhiều điều dưỡng hơn so với nếu không có di cư.

sents.t: Economists call this effect “brain gain”, though its size remains disputed.
sents.vi: Các nhà kinh tế gọi hiệu ứng này là “thu hút chất xám”, dù quy mô của nó vẫn còn tranh cãi.

q.q: The Philippines trains more nurses than its hospitals employ.
Economists agree on the exact size of the “brain gain” effect.
Most Filipino nurses who emigrate return home within ten years.

gram.title: Advanced concession
gram.rule: much as + clause · however + adj / adv + clause · no matter how / what / where · whatever + noun · adjective + as / though + subject + verb (Difficult as it is, …)
gram.note: These structures concede a point while keeping the focus on your main idea, and they are typical of high-band writing. Much as means “although very much”. However hard / no matter how hard emphasise that something does not change the result. The fronted pattern Tempting as it may be, … is formal and elegant; use it sparingly.

ex.t: Much as I admire their courage, I understand the risks they take.
ex.vi: Dù rất ngưỡng mộ lòng can đảm của họ, tôi hiểu rủi ro họ chấp nhận.

ex.t: However hard migrants work, they often face discrimination.

ex.t: No matter where you live, you will miss home at times.
ex.vi: Dù sống ở đâu, đôi lúc bạn vẫn sẽ nhớ nhà.

ex.t: Tempting as it may be, closing borders is not a solution.
ex.vi: Dù có hấp dẫn đến đâu, đóng cửa biên giới không phải là giải pháp.

drill.t: ___ I love travelling, I could not live abroad.

lines.t: Why do people move to other countries?
lines.vi: Vì sao người ta chuyển đến nước khác?

lines.t: Economists usually talk about push and pull factors. Push factors are problems at home — unemployment, conflict, increasingly climate-related disasters — while pull factors are higher wages, safety or better education abroad. In practice, though, most people are influenced by personal networks: they go where relatives have already settled.
lines.vi: Các nhà kinh tế thường nói về yếu tố đẩy và kéo. Yếu tố đẩy là vấn đề ở quê nhà — thất nghiệp, xung đột, ngày càng nhiều thảm hoạ liên quan khí hậu — còn yếu tố kéo là lương cao hơn, an toàn hay giáo dục tốt hơn ở nước ngoài. Tuy nhiên trên thực tế, phần lớn người ta chịu ảnh hưởng của mạng lưới cá nhân: họ đến nơi người thân đã định cư.

lines.t: How does emigration affect the countries people leave?
lines.vi: Di cư ảnh hưởng thế nào đến nước người ta ra đi?

lines.t: It’s mixed. Losing skilled doctors and engineers clearly hurts, especially in small countries. On the other hand, remittances can be a lifeline — in some countries they’re worth more than all foreign aid combined — and returning migrants often bring back skills and investment.
lines.vi: Có cả hai mặt. Mất bác sĩ và kỹ sư giỏi rõ ràng gây thiệt hại, nhất là ở nước nhỏ. Mặt khác, kiều hối có thể là cứu cánh — ở một số nước nó lớn hơn toàn bộ viện trợ nước ngoài cộng lại — và người di cư trở về thường mang theo kỹ năng và vốn đầu tư.

lines.t: What can governments do to help immigrants integrate?
lines.vi: Chính phủ có thể làm gì để giúp người nhập cư hội nhập?

lines.t: Language classes are the obvious starting point, since without the language people get stuck in low-paid work. Recognising foreign qualifications matters too — it’s absurd when a trained doctor ends up driving a taxi. And schools have a big role, because children often integrate first and then help their parents.
lines.vi: Lớp ngôn ngữ là điểm khởi đầu hiển nhiên, vì không có ngôn ngữ người ta bị mắc kẹt trong việc lương thấp. Công nhận bằng cấp nước ngoài cũng quan trọng — thật vô lý khi một bác sĩ được đào tạo bài bản lại đi lái taxi. Và trường học có vai trò lớn, vì trẻ em thường hội nhập trước rồi giúp cha mẹ.

gram2.title: Register: formal verbs vs phrasal verbs
gram2.rule: put up with → tolerate · find out → discover / ascertain · set up → establish · cut down on → reduce · look into → investigate · go up → increase
gram2.note: Phrasal verbs are natural and welcome in Speaking. In Task 2, however, a more formal single-word verb is often better, because it matches the academic register. Not every phrasal verb is informal — “carry out” and “point out” are fine in essays — but avoid chatty ones like “get rid of” or “put up with” in formal writing.

ex.vi: Các nhà nghiên cứu điều tra tác động của kiều hối.

ex.t: Visa fees have increased sharply.
ex.vi: Phí thị thực tăng mạnh.

cue.card: Describe someone you know who moved to another country.
points: and explain how you feel about their decision
model: I’d like to talk about my friend Minh, who moved to Melbourne about six years ago. We were at university together, and he was always the most ambitious person in our class.

He went initially as a postgraduate student in environmental engineering, partly because there were very few programmes in his specialism back home, and partly — he’d admit this himself — for a change of scenery. After graduating, he found work at a consultancy that designs flood defences, and he’s now applied for permanent residency.

His life has changed in almost every way. Professionally, he’s working on projects far larger than he could have here, and he earns substantially more. But it hasn’t been easy. For the first year he worked evenings in a restaurant to cover his rent, and he told me that however good his English was on paper, he struggled to understand jokes in meetings, which made him feel like an outsider. I have mixed feelings about his decision. Much as I’m proud of him, it does feel like a small example of the brain drain — his skills in flood management would be extremely valuable in the Mekong Delta. He says he plans to come back eventually, though, and bring that experience with him, so perhaps it will turn out to be a brain gain after all.

write.prompt: In many countries, an increasing number of skilled workers are moving abroad to work. What problems does this cause for their home countries, and what can be done to address them?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase + outline (problems: skill shortages, lost investment, weaker services; solutions: pay and conditions, circular migration, diaspora engagement)
Body 1: problems — specific sectors (health), lost public investment in education, knock-on effects
Body 2: solutions — improve conditions; bilateral agreements and return incentives; use the diaspora
Conclusion: summarise; migration can be turned into a benefit
model: The emigration of skilled professionals, such as doctors, engineers and IT specialists, has accelerated in many developing countries. This trend creates serious difficulties for the countries they leave behind, most notably shortages in vital services and the loss of public investment in education, but these problems can be mitigated through better working conditions, managed migration schemes and stronger links with citizens abroad.

The most immediate problem is a shortage of skills in key sectors. When large numbers of nurses or doctors emigrate, hospitals, particularly in rural areas, are left understaffed, and patients bear the brunt of longer waiting times and lower-quality care. A second issue is financial: governments often subsidise the education of these professionals heavily, so when graduates move abroad, the receiving country effectively benefits from that investment without having paid for it. Over time, the departure of the most talented and entrepreneurial individuals may also slow innovation and economic development.

Several measures could address these problems. Firstly, home governments can reduce the incentive to leave by improving salaries, career progression and working conditions in sectors with critical shortages, since pay is rarely the only reason professionals emigrate. Secondly, sending and receiving countries could negotiate agreements whereby workers migrate for fixed periods and then return, bringing back experience, or whereby wealthy countries contribute to training costs. Finally, governments should actively engage their diaspora, for instance by offering tax incentives for returning professionals or creating programmes in which overseas experts teach or advise remotely.

In conclusion, the emigration of skilled workers can deprive home countries of essential expertise and public investment. However, rather than attempting to prevent people from leaving, which is neither practical nor fair, governments should make staying more attractive and build structures that allow migrants’ skills and resources to flow back home.

units.goal: Debate higher education funding and outcomes, using information structure and language of proportion.

lines.t: What did you study at university?
lines.vi: Bạn học gì ở đại học?

lines.t: Civil engineering. It was a five-year course, and honestly the bulk of what I use at work now I learned during my internship rather than in lectures.
lines.vi: Kỹ thuật xây dựng. Đó là khoá năm năm, và thật lòng phần lớn những gì tôi dùng trong công việc giờ tôi học được trong kỳ thực tập chứ không phải trên giảng đường.

lines.t: Would you like to study again in the future?
lines.vi: Bạn có muốn đi học lại trong tương lai không?

lines.t: Yes, probably a part-time master’s in project management. I’d rather upskill while working than stop for two years.
lines.vi: Có, có lẽ là thạc sĩ quản lý dự án bán thời gian. Tôi muốn nâng cao kỹ năng trong khi đi làm hơn là nghỉ hai năm.

lines.t: Is university popular among young people in your country?
lines.vi: Đại học có phổ biến với người trẻ ở nước bạn không?

lines.t: Extremely. Many families see a degree as essential, almost regardless of the subject. I think that’s starting to change, though, as more graduates find themselves overqualified for the jobs available.
lines.vi: Cực kỳ phổ biến. Nhiều gia đình coi bằng đại học là thiết yếu, gần như bất kể ngành gì. Tôi nghĩ điều đó đang bắt đầu thay đổi khi ngày càng nhiều người tốt nghiệp thấy mình thừa trình độ so với công việc có sẵn.

read.title: Is a degree still worth it?

sents.t: On average, graduates in most OECD countries earn around 50 per cent more than people with only a secondary education.
sents.vi: Trung bình, người tốt nghiệp đại học ở hầu hết các nước OECD kiếm nhiều hơn khoảng 50% so với người chỉ học hết trung học.

sents.t: However, this average hides large differences between subjects and institutions.
sents.vi: Tuy nhiên, con số trung bình này che giấu khác biệt lớn giữa các ngành và trường.

sents.t: Graduates in medicine, engineering and economics typically see the highest returns, while some arts degrees show almost no earnings advantage.
sents.vi: Người tốt nghiệp y, kỹ thuật và kinh tế thường có lợi tức cao nhất, trong khi một số ngành nghệ thuật gần như không có lợi thế thu nhập.

sents.t: Moreover, part of the premium may reflect the abilities that graduates had before university, rather than what they learned there.
sents.vi: Hơn nữa, một phần chênh lệch có thể phản ánh năng lực người tốt nghiệp đã có trước khi vào đại học, chứ không phải điều họ học được ở đó.

sents.t: Researchers find it difficult to separate these two effects precisely.
sents.vi: Các nhà nghiên cứu thấy khó tách biệt chính xác hai tác động này.

q.q: Graduates earn about half as much again as people with only secondary education, on average.
All degree subjects provide a similar earnings advantage.
Arts graduates are more satisfied with their jobs than engineering graduates.

gram.title: Information structure: given before new
gram.rule: Start with known information, end with new · use this / such / these to link back · front a time or contrast phrase · passive to keep the topic as subject
gram.note: Coherent writing usually places familiar information at the start of a sentence and new, important information at the end. If the previous sentence ended with “tuition fees”, the next can begin “These fees …”. The passive helps keep the same topic in subject position: Universities receive public money. They are also funded by fees. This principle matters more for band 7+ coherence than adding more linking words.

ex.t: Many students now borrow to pay fees. This debt can take decades to repay.
ex.vi: Nhiều sinh viên giờ vay để đóng học phí. Khoản nợ này có thể mất hàng chục năm để trả.

ex.t: Universities are expanding quickly. Such rapid growth raises concerns about quality.
ex.vi: Các trường đại học đang mở rộng nhanh. Sự tăng trưởng nhanh như vậy làm dấy lên lo ngại về chất lượng.

ex.t: The scheme was introduced in 2015. Since then, enrolment has doubled.
ex.vi: Chương trình được áp dụng năm 2015. Kể từ đó, số nhập học tăng gấp đôi.

ex.t: Apprenticeships are popular in Germany, where they are respected by employers.
ex.vi: Học việc phổ biến ở Đức, nơi chúng được nhà tuyển dụng tôn trọng.

lines.t: Should university education be free for everyone?
lines.vi: Giáo dục đại học có nên miễn phí cho mọi người?

lines.t: I’m not convinced it should be free for everyone, because the benefits are partly private — graduates earn more. But no talented student should be excluded because of cost. A system of means-tested grants, or loans that are only repaid above a certain salary, seems fairer than either extreme.
lines.vi: Tôi không tin nó nên miễn phí cho tất cả, vì lợi ích một phần là cá nhân — người tốt nghiệp kiếm nhiều hơn. Nhưng không sinh viên giỏi nào nên bị loại vì chi phí. Hệ thống trợ cấp theo thu nhập, hoặc khoản vay chỉ phải trả khi lương vượt một mức nhất định, có vẻ công bằng hơn hai thái cực.

lines.t: Are too many young people going to university?
lines.vi: Có quá nhiều người trẻ vào đại học không?

lines.t: In some countries, arguably yes. If a degree becomes the default, employers start demanding one for jobs that never required it, and young people spend years and money just to stay in the same place. Strong apprenticeships, like Germany’s, give a respected alternative.
lines.vi: Ở một số nước, có thể nói là có. Nếu bằng đại học trở thành mặc định, nhà tuyển dụng bắt đầu đòi hỏi nó cho những việc vốn không cần, và người trẻ tốn nhiều năm và tiền chỉ để đứng yên một chỗ. Chương trình học việc mạnh như ở Đức mang lại một lựa chọn thay thế được tôn trọng.

lines.t: What is the main purpose of a university?
lines.vi: Mục đích chính của đại học là gì?

lines.t: I’d say there are two, and they’re in tension. One is to train people for skilled work; the other is to produce knowledge and teach people to think independently. A good university protects the second even when the first gets most of the attention.
lines.vi: Tôi cho là có hai, và chúng có phần mâu thuẫn. Một là đào tạo người cho công việc chuyên môn; hai là tạo ra tri thức và dạy người ta tư duy độc lập. Một trường đại học tốt bảo vệ mục đích thứ hai ngay cả khi mục đích thứ nhất được chú ý nhiều hơn.

gram2.title: Expressing proportion
gram2.rule: a fraction of · the bulk of / the vast majority of · a disproportionate share / number of · one in five · roughly a third · the remainder
gram2.note: Precise proportion language lets you discuss data in both Task 1 and Task 2 without listing every number. A fraction of means a small part. The bulk of means most. Disproportionate signals unfairness: a share bigger (or smaller) than expected. Use one in + number for memorable statistics.

cue.card: Describe a course or training you took that was useful.
points: when and where you took it
and explain why it was useful
model: The most useful course I’ve taken wasn’t at university at all. It was a six-week evening course in technical writing that my company paid for about three years ago, run by a former journalist who now trains engineers.

I signed up somewhat reluctantly, because I assumed I could already write reasonably well. The first session changed my mind. She gave us one of our own real reports, and within ten minutes she’d shown that the key recommendation was buried on page seven, after pages of background nobody would read. From then on, each week focused on one principle: putting the conclusion first, writing for a specific reader, cutting sentences in half, and using tables instead of long paragraphs of numbers.

It was useful in a very direct way. Within a few months, my manager mentioned that my reports were the only ones clients actually responded to quickly, and I think that contributed to my promotion the following year. But it also changed how I think. Clear writing forces clear thinking — if you can’t state your main point in one sentence, you probably haven’t worked out what it is. In some ways, that course gave me a better return on investment than a fraction of my degree did, which says something about how valuable short, practical training can be.

write.prompt: The bar chart below shows the percentage of 25–34-year-olds with a university degree in five countries in 2000 and 2020. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
write.data:
Country        2000   2020
South Korea     37%    70%
Canada          48%    63%
UK              29%    52%
Germany         22%    33%
Italy           10%    29%
plan: Introduction: paraphrase (percentage of 25–34-year-olds with a degree → proportion of young adults who had completed higher education)
Overview: all five rose; South Korea overtook Canada to lead; Italy and Germany remained lowest
Body 1: South Korea and Canada — the leaders; size of rise
Body 2: UK, Germany, Italy — UK’s strong growth; Italy nearly tripled but still lowest; Germany smallest absolute rise (link to apprenticeships is not in data — avoid speculation)
model: The bar chart compares the proportion of young adults aged 25 to 34 who held a university degree in five countries in 2000 and 2020.

Overall, the figure increased in every country over the twenty-year period, although there were considerable differences in both the scale of growth and the final levels. South Korea experienced the most rapid expansion and had overtaken Canada to rank first by 2020, while Italy and Germany remained at the bottom of the group.

In 2000, Canada had the highest proportion of graduates, at almost half of the age group (48%), compared with just over a third in South Korea. Over the following two decades, however, the Korean figure nearly doubled to 70%, the highest of the five countries, whereas the Canadian rate rose more modestly to 63%.

Among the remaining countries, the UK saw substantial growth, from 29% to just over half of young adults. Italy began from by far the lowest base, with only one in ten young people holding a degree in 2000, and although this proportion almost tripled to 29%, it was still the lowest in 2020. Germany recorded the smallest increase, of eleven percentage points, reaching a third of the age group.

units.title: Public health & lifestyle diseases
units.goal: Evaluate government action on diet, smoking and exercise, using causatives and rebuttal language.

lines.t: Has your diet changed in recent years?
lines.vi: Chế độ ăn của bạn có thay đổi mấy năm gần đây không?

lines.t: Quite a lot. I used to rely on instant noodles and sugary iced coffee, but after I had my cholesterol checked and the results were borderline, I started cooking at home most evenings.
lines.vi: Khá nhiều. Tôi từng sống nhờ mì gói và cà phê đá nhiều đường, nhưng sau khi đi kiểm tra mỡ máu và kết quả ở mức ranh giới, tôi bắt đầu nấu ăn ở nhà hầu hết các tối.

lines.t: Do you get enough exercise?
lines.vi: Bạn có tập thể dục đủ không?

lines.t: Probably not, if I’m honest. My job is very sedentary, so I’ve started cycling to work twice a week, which at least forces me to move.
lines.vi: Thật lòng thì có lẽ chưa. Công việc của tôi rất ít vận động, nên tôi bắt đầu đạp xe đi làm hai lần một tuần, ít nhất buộc tôi phải vận động.

lines.t: Do you read food labels?
lines.vi: Bạn có đọc nhãn thực phẩm không?

lines.t: I do now, mainly for sugar. It was quite a shock to discover how much is added to things that don’t even taste sweet, like bread and sauces.
lines.vi: Giờ thì có, chủ yếu để xem lượng đường. Khá sốc khi phát hiện bao nhiêu đường được thêm vào những thứ thậm chí không có vị ngọt, như bánh mì và nước sốt.

sents.t: In 2018, the United Kingdom introduced a tax on soft drinks containing more than five grams of sugar per 100 millilitres.
sents.vi: Năm 2018, Vương quốc Anh áp thuế với nước ngọt chứa hơn năm gam đường mỗi 100 ml.

sents.t: Because the tax was announced two years in advance, many manufacturers reformulated their products before it took effect.
sents.vi: Vì thuế được công bố trước hai năm, nhiều nhà sản xuất đã điều chỉnh công thức sản phẩm trước khi thuế có hiệu lực.

sents.t: As a result, the amount of sugar sold in soft drinks fell by almost 30 per cent, while total sales remained roughly stable.
sents.vi: Kết quả là lượng đường bán ra trong nước ngọt giảm gần 30%, trong khi tổng doanh số gần như ổn định.

sents.t: Some studies have also linked the tax to a small reduction in obesity among girls aged ten to eleven.
sents.vi: Một số nghiên cứu còn liên hệ thuế này với sự giảm nhẹ béo phì ở bé gái 10–11 tuổi.

sents.t: Critics, however, point out that sugar consumption from other foods has not changed significantly.
sents.vi: Tuy nhiên, những người phê bình chỉ ra rằng lượng đường tiêu thụ từ các thực phẩm khác không thay đổi đáng kể.

q.q: Many companies changed their recipes before the tax started.
Total soft drink sales fell by about 30 per cent.
The tax was later extended to sweets and cakes.

gram.title: Causative structures
gram.rule: have / get + object + past participle (have something done) · make + someone + verb · force / require / compel / oblige + someone + to + verb · let / allow + someone
gram.note: Causatives describe who causes an action. Have something done means you arrange for someone else to do it: I had my eyes tested. In policy discussions, the verbs require, compel, oblige and force + object + to-infinitive express rules and laws precisely: The law requires manufacturers to label sugar content. Note: make + object + bare infinitive (no to).

ex.t: I have my blood pressure checked every six months.
ex.vi: Tôi đi đo huyết áp sáu tháng một lần.

ex.t: The law requires restaurants to display calorie counts.
ex.vi: Luật yêu cầu nhà hàng ghi lượng calo.

ex.t: Some companies let staff exercise during working hours.

lines.t: Should governments tax unhealthy food?
lines.vi: Chính phủ có nên đánh thuế thực phẩm không lành mạnh?

lines.t: I think targeted taxes can work, as the UK sugar tax suggests — especially when they push companies to reformulate products rather than just making people pay more. Critics contend that these taxes are regressive, which is true, but poorer families also suffer most from diet-related illness, so they may benefit most as well.
lines.vi: Tôi nghĩ thuế có mục tiêu có thể hiệu quả, như thuế đường ở Anh cho thấy — nhất là khi nó thúc các công ty điều chỉnh công thức chứ không chỉ khiến người dân trả nhiều hơn. Những người phản đối cho rằng các loại thuế này mang tính luỹ thoái, điều đó đúng, nhưng gia đình nghèo cũng chịu nhiều nhất bệnh tật do ăn uống, nên họ có thể cũng được lợi nhiều nhất.

lines.t: Isn’t health a matter of personal responsibility?
lines.vi: Sức khoẻ không phải là trách nhiệm cá nhân sao?

lines.t: Partly, but that argument overlooks how much our choices are shaped by our environment. If the cheapest, most heavily advertised food is unhealthy and there’s nowhere safe to walk, telling people to “choose better” isn’t enough. Personal responsibility works best when the healthy option is also the easy one.
lines.vi: Một phần, nhưng lập luận đó bỏ qua việc lựa chọn của ta bị môi trường định hình đến mức nào. Nếu thức ăn rẻ nhất, được quảng cáo nhiều nhất lại không lành mạnh và chẳng có chỗ nào an toàn để đi bộ, bảo người ta “hãy chọn tốt hơn” là không đủ. Trách nhiệm cá nhân hiệu quả nhất khi lựa chọn lành mạnh cũng là lựa chọn dễ dàng.

lines.t: How can employers improve their staff’s health?
lines.vi: Doanh nghiệp có thể cải thiện sức khoẻ nhân viên thế nào?

lines.t: Small nudges help — standing desks, healthier canteen food, showers so people can cycle in. But the biggest factor is probably working hours. Exhausted employees don’t have the energy to cook or exercise, whatever the company offers.
lines.vi: Những gợi ý nhỏ có ích — bàn đứng, căng tin lành mạnh hơn, nhà tắm để người ta đạp xe đến. Nhưng yếu tố lớn nhất có lẽ là giờ làm việc. Nhân viên kiệt sức sẽ không còn sức nấu ăn hay tập luyện, bất kể công ty cung cấp gì.

gram2.title: Presenting and rebutting counter-arguments
gram2.rule: Critics / Opponents contend that … · It could be objected that … · However, this view overlooks … · While this concern is understandable, … · This argument fails to take into account …
gram2.note: A band 7+ essay often includes a counter-argument followed by a rebuttal. First state the opposing view fairly, using a neutral reporting verb. Then show its weakness with phrases such as this overlooks or fails to take into account. A good rebuttal gives a reason or evidence, not just disagreement.

ex.t: Opponents contend that the tax restricts freedom of choice.

ex.t: However, this view overlooks the influence of marketing on children.

ex.t: While this concern is understandable, the evidence suggests otherwise.
ex.vi: Dù mối lo này dễ hiểu, bằng chứng lại cho thấy điều ngược lại.

ex.t: This argument fails to take into account the cost to the health system.
ex.vi: Lập luận này không tính đến chi phí cho hệ thống y tế.

cue.card: Describe a change you made to become healthier.
points: when and why you made it
and explain what effect it has had
model: The change I’d like to talk about is cutting down drastically on sugary drinks — in my case, the iced milk coffee and bubble tea I was drinking two or three times a day.

I made the decision about two years ago, after a routine health check at work. The doctor wasn’t alarmed, but my blood sugar was at the upper end of normal, and she asked me how many sweet drinks I had a day. When I actually counted, it came to roughly fifteen teaspoons of sugar, which shocked me, because I never thought of myself as someone with a sweet tooth.

It was harder than I expected. For the first couple of weeks, I had headaches in the afternoon and I really missed the ritual of going out for a drink with colleagues. What helped was not quitting completely but making small substitutions: I switched to black coffee with a little condensed milk, then to unsweetened tea, and I’d have bubble tea only at weekends. The effect has been surprisingly significant. I’ve lost about four kilos without changing anything else, my energy is more stable in the afternoons, and at my last check-up my blood sugar was comfortably in the normal range. It also made me realise how much of what we eat is shaped by habit and social routine rather than real choice.

write.prompt: Some people think that governments should be responsible for making sure their citizens are healthy, for example by taxing unhealthy food. Others believe that health is a matter of personal responsibility. Discuss both views and give your opinion.
plan: Introduction: paraphrase both views + position (shared, but government must shape the environment)
Body 1: personal responsibility — autonomy, nanny state, regressive taxes; fair representation
Body 2: government role — environment shapes choice, marketing, cost to health system, evidence from sugar and tobacco
Conclusion: rebut the autonomy argument and restate shared-responsibility view
model: Rising rates of obesity, diabetes and heart disease have prompted debate about who is responsible for people’s health. While some argue that governments should intervene actively, for instance through taxes on unhealthy products, others insist that what people eat and how they live is a matter of personal choice. In my view, individuals bear some responsibility, but governments have a duty to create conditions in which healthy choices are realistic for everyone.

Those who emphasise personal responsibility make valid points. Adults are generally entitled to make decisions about their own lives, even unwise ones, and policies that dictate what people should eat can be seen as an example of the “nanny state”. Opponents of food taxes also contend that such measures are regressive, since low-income households spend a larger share of their income on food and would therefore be hit hardest. From this perspective, education and information are preferable to taxation or restrictions.

However, this view overlooks the extent to which individual choices are shaped by the environment. Unhealthy products are often the cheapest and most heavily marketed, and many people, particularly children, are exposed to persuasive advertising long before they can evaluate it critically. In addition, poor health is not purely a private matter: treating preventable illnesses places an enormous strain on public health systems funded by all taxpayers. There is also clear evidence that government action can work. Tobacco taxes and advertising bans have contributed to dramatic falls in smoking, and the UK’s tax on sugary drinks led manufacturers to cut sugar content by nearly 30 per cent without reducing sales.

In conclusion, while people should take responsibility for their own lifestyles, I believe this is only reasonable if healthy options are affordable and accessible. Governments should therefore use measures such as targeted taxes, clear labelling and limits on marketing to children, ideally combined with subsidies for fruit and vegetables so that the poorest households benefit rather than lose out.
