cue.card: Describe a famous person whose behaviour you disagreed with.
points: and explain why you disagreed with their behaviour
model: I’d like to talk about a well-known lifestyle influencer — I won’t name her — who has several million followers, mostly young women, and who was involved in a controversy last year.

She promoted a slimming tea in a series of videos, claiming she had lost five kilos in two weeks simply by drinking it. Several viewers later found that the product contained an undeclared laxative, and a few reported health problems. It also emerged that her “before” photos had been taken years earlier.

The reaction was intense. Many followers felt betrayed and left angry comments; a consumer group reported the product to the authorities; and two other brands ended their endorsement deals with her. She issued a public apology, but many people felt it was perceived as insincere, because she blamed her management team rather than taking responsibility.

I disagreed with her behaviour for two reasons. Firstly, she must have known her audience was young and impressionable, so she should have been far more careful about promoting anything health-related. Secondly, she could easily have checked the ingredients or asked a doctor before accepting the deal. I don’t think influencers need to be perfect role models, but when your income depends on people trusting you, honesty isn’t optional.

write.prompt: Many young people today want to become famous, for example as influencers or celebrities. Why is this? Is it a positive or negative development?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase; answer — mainly negative
Body 1: reasons — social media visibility, perceived easy wealth and status, decline of traditional routes, recognition need
Body 2: evaluation — some positives (creativity, entrepreneurship), but negatives outweigh: unrealistic odds, mental health, values
Conclusion
model: A striking number of young people now name fame, whether as social media influencers, singers or actors, as a major ambition. This essay will examine the reasons for this trend and argue that, although it has some positive aspects, it is largely a negative development.

The most obvious explanation is the rise of social media. Platforms such as TikTok and YouTube make celebrity seem accessible: young people regularly see peers who have gained huge audiences from ordinary bedrooms, and algorithms can turn an unknown person into a star overnight. Moreover, fame is perceived as a shortcut to wealth and status at a time when traditional routes, such as a university degree followed by a stable career, appear less reliable and housing increasingly unaffordable. Finally, in a culture that measures popularity in likes and followers, it is perhaps unsurprising that adolescents, who naturally seek recognition, see fame as a sign of personal worth.

There are some positive aspects to this trend. Content creation can develop genuine skills in filming, editing, writing and marketing, and some young creators have built successful small businesses. Nevertheless, I believe the drawbacks are more significant. For the overwhelming majority, the odds of earning a living from fame are extremely low, and time invested in chasing followers may come at the expense of education or more realistic career paths. The pursuit of attention can also damage mental health, as self-esteem becomes dependent on fluctuating online approval, and those who do become famous often face intense public scrutiny and harassment. More broadly, a culture in which visibility is valued above achievement may encourage shallow values.

In conclusion, the desire for fame among young people is driven by social media, economic uncertainty and the need for recognition. While it can foster creativity and entrepreneurship, its effects on young people’s prospects and wellbeing make it, on balance, a negative development.

lines.t: Do you remember any adverts from your childhood?
lines.vi: Bạn có nhớ quảng cáo nào thời thơ ấu không?

lines.t: Very clearly — a milk advert with a cartoon cow mascot and a catchy song. I nagged my mother to buy that brand for years, which is pester power in action, I suppose.
lines.vi: Rất rõ — quảng cáo sữa có linh vật bò hoạt hình và bài hát bắt tai. Tôi nài mẹ mua hãng đó suốt nhiều năm, có lẽ đó chính là sức ép nài nỉ.

lines.t: Where do children see adverts today?
lines.vi: Ngày nay trẻ em xem quảng cáo ở đâu?

lines.t: Mostly on YouTube and in mobile games. My nephew watches unboxing videos that are basically long adverts, though he doesn’t realise it.
lines.vi: Chủ yếu trên YouTube và trong game điện thoại. Cháu tôi xem video đập hộp thực chất là quảng cáo dài, dù cháu không nhận ra.

lines.t: Do adverts influence what you buy?
lines.vi: Quảng cáo có ảnh hưởng đến việc bạn mua gì không?

lines.t: Less than they used to, because I tend to read reviews. But I’m sure they influence me in ways I don’t notice — that’s rather the point of them.
lines.vi: Ít hơn trước, vì tôi hay đọc đánh giá. Nhưng chắc chắn chúng ảnh hưởng tôi theo cách tôi không nhận thấy — đó chính là mục đích của chúng.

sents.t: Research suggests that most children under the age of about eight cannot reliably distinguish adverts from programmes.
sents.vi: Nghiên cứu cho thấy phần lớn trẻ dưới khoảng tám tuổi không phân biệt được quảng cáo với chương trình.

sents.t: Even older children, who know that adverts exist, often fail to understand their persuasive intent.
sents.vi: Ngay cả trẻ lớn hơn, dù biết quảng cáo tồn tại, thường không hiểu được ý đồ thuyết phục.

sents.t: Online, the boundaries are even less clear, as products appear inside games, videos made by child influencers and interactive apps.
sents.vi: Trên mạng, ranh giới còn mờ hơn, khi sản phẩm xuất hiện trong game, video của người có ảnh hưởng nhí và ứng dụng tương tác.

sents.t: Quebec has banned commercial advertising aimed at under-thirteens since 1980, and researchers have linked the ban to lower fast-food spending among French-speaking families.
sents.vi: Quebec cấm quảng cáo thương mại nhắm vào trẻ dưới mười ba tuổi từ năm 1980, và nhà nghiên cứu liên hệ lệnh cấm với chi tiêu đồ ăn nhanh thấp hơn ở các gia đình nói tiếng Pháp.

sents.t: However, such bans are difficult to enforce on global platforms.
sents.vi: Tuy nhiên, các lệnh cấm như vậy khó thực thi trên nền tảng toàn cầu.

q.q: Most young children can easily tell adverts from programmes.
Quebec’s ban on advertising to children began in 1980.

gram.title: Noun clauses as subjects
gram.rule: What + clause · Whether + clause · How / Why + clause · The fact that + clause … + verb
gram.note: A whole clause can act as the subject of a sentence, creating the complex structures typical of band 8 writing: What concerns parents most is the hidden nature of online advertising. Whether a ban would work remains unclear. The fact that children cannot recognise adverts makes them vulnerable. The verb after a noun clause is singular.

lines.t: Should advertising aimed at children be banned?
lines.vi: Có nên cấm quảng cáo nhắm vào trẻ em không?

lines.t: For young children, I think so, at least for junk food and gambling-like features such as loot boxes. The fact that small children can’t recognise persuasive intent means advertising to them is inherently unfair. For teenagers, I’d favour strict rules and media literacy rather than an outright ban.
lines.vi: Với trẻ nhỏ, tôi nghĩ là nên, ít nhất với đồ ăn vặt và tính năng giống cờ bạc như hộp quà ngẫu nhiên. Việc trẻ nhỏ không nhận ra ý đồ thuyết phục khiến quảng cáo nhắm vào chúng vốn đã bất công. Với thiếu niên, tôi ủng hộ quy định chặt và giáo dục truyền thông hơn là cấm hoàn toàn.

lines.t: Isn’t it the parents’ job to control what children see?
lines.vi: Kiểm soát những gì trẻ xem chẳng phải là việc của cha mẹ sao?

lines.t: Parents certainly have a role, but it’s an unequal contest. Companies employ psychologists and data scientists to capture children’s attention, while parents are often busy working. What seems reasonable is shared responsibility, with regulation setting the boundaries.
lines.vi: Cha mẹ chắc chắn có vai trò, nhưng đó là cuộc đấu không cân sức. Doanh nghiệp thuê nhà tâm lý và nhà khoa học dữ liệu để thu hút sự chú ý của trẻ, trong khi cha mẹ thường bận đi làm. Điều có vẻ hợp lý là chia sẻ trách nhiệm, với luật pháp vạch ranh giới.

lines.t: Are children today more materialistic than in the past?
lines.vi: Trẻ em ngày nay có trọng vật chất hơn trước không?

lines.t: It’s hard to measure, but they’re certainly exposed to far more marketing, and it’s more personalised. Whether that makes them more materialistic probably depends on the values they see at home.
lines.vi: Khó đo lường, nhưng chắc chắn chúng tiếp xúc nhiều quảng cáo hơn và được cá nhân hoá hơn. Điều đó có khiến chúng trọng vật chất hơn không có lẽ tuỳ vào giá trị chúng thấy ở nhà.

cue.card: Describe an advertisement that you think was effective.
points: and explain why you think it was effective
model: I’d like to talk about a Tết advertisement for a well-known motorbike brand that went viral in Vietnam a few years ago.
I first saw it on YouTube, but it was later shown on television and shared endlessly on Facebook in the weeks before the New Year.

The story followed an elderly father in the countryside preparing for Tết, cleaning the house and cooking his son’s favourite dishes, only to receive a call saying his son couldn’t come home because of work. Then, on the last evening of the year, he hears a motorbike outside, and his son walks in, having ridden all the way from the city. The product barely appeared — just a few seconds at the end with the slogan.

What made it effective, I think, was that it sold an emotion rather than a machine. Millions of young Vietnamese work far from home and feel guilty about not visiting their parents often enough, so it touched a very sensitive nerve. The fact that the brand was almost invisible made it feel less like an advert and more like a short film, which is why people shared it voluntarily. Of course, looking back, I can see how cleverly it manipulated our feelings — but that is precisely why it worked.

write.prompt: Advertising aimed at children should be banned. To what extent do you agree or disagree?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase; position — agree for young children and harmful products; regulation for older children
Body 1: arguments for a ban — cannot recognise persuasive intent, junk food and obesity, pester power and family conflict, hidden online ads
Body 2: counter-arguments — enforcement, funding of children’s content, teenagers’ autonomy, parents’ role
Body 3: balanced solution
Conclusion
model: Children today are exposed to an unprecedented amount of advertising, not only on television but in games, apps and videos made by influencers. Some argue that advertising directed at children should be prohibited entirely. I agree that a ban is justified for young children and for harmful products, but I believe that for older children strict regulation combined with education is more realistic.

The central argument for a ban is one of fairness. Research consistently shows that young children cannot reliably distinguish adverts from entertainment, let alone understand their persuasive intent. Advertising to them therefore exploits a vulnerability rather than informing a choice. The consequences can be serious: marketing of sugary snacks and fast food has been linked to childhood obesity, and pester power creates conflict between children and parents, particularly in low-income families. Online, the problem is magnified, since products are embedded in games, unboxing videos and loot boxes that resemble gambling.

Nevertheless, a total ban raises practical difficulties. Global platforms are hard to regulate at a national level, and determined marketers may simply shift to less visible methods such as product placement. Advertising revenue also funds much children’s television and many free educational apps. Moreover, teenagers are capable of understanding marketing, and treating them as completely unable to judge may be counterproductive.

What seems most sensible, therefore, is a graduated approach. Governments should ban all advertising aimed at children under around twelve, as Quebec and Sweden have done, and prohibit the promotion of junk food and gambling-like mechanics to all minors. For older children, clear labelling of paid content, limits on personal data collection and media literacy teaching in schools would help them recognise and resist manipulation.

In conclusion, I agree that advertising aimed at young children should be banned, as it is inherently unfair. For teenagers, however, robust regulation and education offer a more workable solution than an outright prohibition.

units.title: Car ownership & urban mobility
units.goal: Discuss cars, motorbikes and public transport in growing cities, using reduced relative clauses and the language of trade-offs.

lines.t: How do you usually travel around your city?
lines.vi: Bạn thường đi lại trong thành phố bằng gì?

lines.t: By motorbike, like most people here. I’ve started taking the new metro line on days when it rains, though, because it’s air-conditioned and avoids the gridlock.
lines.vi: Bằng xe máy, như phần lớn mọi người ở đây. Nhưng tôi bắt đầu đi tuyến metro mới vào những hôm mưa, vì có điều hoà và tránh được tắc đường.

lines.t: Would you like to own a car?
lines.vi: Bạn có muốn sở hữu ô tô không?

lines.t: For long trips with my family, yes, but for daily life in the city it doesn’t make much sense. Parking spaces are scarce and expensive, and a car would spend most of the day stuck in traffic.
lines.vi: Cho chuyến đi xa với gia đình thì có, nhưng với đời sống hằng ngày ở thành phố thì không hợp lý lắm. Chỗ đỗ xe khan hiếm và đắt, và ô tô sẽ kẹt xe phần lớn thời gian.

lines.t: Has transport in your city improved recently?
lines.vi: Giao thông ở thành phố bạn gần đây có cải thiện không?

lines.t: Somewhat. The metro was a big step, and there are more electric buses. But the last-mile problem remains — the walk from the station to my office is along a pavement full of parked motorbikes.
lines.vi: Có phần. Metro là bước tiến lớn, và có thêm xe buýt điện. Nhưng chặng cuối vẫn là vấn đề — đường đi bộ từ ga đến văn phòng tôi là vỉa hè đầy xe máy đỗ.

sents.t: For decades, the standard response to congestion was to build wider roads.
sents.vi: Trong nhiều thập kỷ, giải pháp tiêu chuẩn cho ùn tắc là xây đường rộng hơn.

sents.t: Transport researchers now widely accept that this tends to make traffic worse in the long run, a phenomenon known as induced demand.
sents.vi: Các nhà nghiên cứu giao thông nay thừa nhận rộng rãi rằng điều này có xu hướng làm giao thông tệ hơn về lâu dài, hiện tượng gọi là nhu cầu phát sinh.

sents.t: When a road becomes faster, people who previously avoided it start driving, and within a few years it is congested again.
sents.vi: Khi một con đường nhanh hơn, những người trước đây tránh nó bắt đầu lái xe vào, và vài năm sau nó lại ùn tắc.

sents.t: Cities such as Seoul have gone in the opposite direction, removing a major elevated highway and replacing it with a stream and park.
sents.vi: Những thành phố như Seoul đi theo hướng ngược lại, dỡ bỏ một đường cao tốc trên cao và thay bằng dòng suối và công viên.

sents.t: Contrary to predictions, traffic in the surrounding area did not increase significantly.
sents.vi: Trái với dự đoán, giao thông khu vực xung quanh không tăng đáng kể.

q.q: Building wider roads usually solves congestion permanently.
Seoul replaced a highway with a stream and park.
Seoul’s project was mainly funded by private companies.

gram.title: Reduced relative clauses
gram.rule: noun + -ing (= who/which + active verb) · noun + past participle (= who/which + passive verb)
gram.note: Removing “who/which + be” makes noun phrases more compact and academic: Commuters travelling by car (= who travel) spend hours in traffic. Roads built in the 1990s (= which were built) are now overcrowded. Use -ing for active meaning and a past participle for passive meaning.

lines.t: Why do many people still prefer private vehicles to public transport?
lines.vi: Vì sao nhiều người vẫn thích phương tiện cá nhân hơn giao thông công cộng?

lines.t: Mainly convenience and reliability. In cities where public transport is patchy, a motorbike takes you door to door. There’s also the status factor — in many developing countries, a car is a visible sign of success.
lines.vi: Chủ yếu là tiện và đáng tin. Ở thành phố nơi giao thông công cộng chắp vá, xe máy đưa bạn tận cửa. Còn yếu tố địa vị — ở nhiều nước đang phát triển, ô tô là dấu hiệu thành công rõ ràng.

lines.t: Should governments make driving more expensive?
lines.vi: Chính phủ có nên khiến việc lái xe đắt hơn không?

lines.t: Congestion charges have worked in places like London and Stockholm, but only because they came with good alternatives. Charging people without offering decent public transport would simply punish those who have no choice, so the sequence matters.
lines.vi: Phí chống ùn tắc đã hiệu quả ở London và Stockholm, nhưng chỉ vì đi kèm lựa chọn thay thế tốt. Thu phí mà không có giao thông công cộng tử tế chỉ trừng phạt người không có lựa chọn, nên trình tự rất quan trọng.

lines.t: What will urban transport look like in thirty years?
lines.vi: Giao thông đô thị ba mươi năm nữa sẽ thế nào?

lines.t: I’d guess fewer people will own cars, especially in big cities, with more car-sharing, electric vehicles and metro systems. Whether self-driving cars reduce traffic or simply create more of it is the big unknown.
lines.vi: Tôi đoán sẽ ít người sở hữu ô tô hơn, nhất là ở thành phố lớn, với nhiều dịch vụ dùng chung xe, xe điện và metro hơn. Xe tự lái giảm giao thông hay chỉ tạo thêm là ẩn số lớn.

gram2.title: The language of trade-offs
gram2.rule: at the expense of · come at a cost · in exchange for · strike a balance between … and … · weigh … against …
gram2.note: Band 8 answers show awareness that policies involve trade-offs. These phrases help you express it precisely: Roads were widened at the expense of pavements. Convenience comes at a cost to the environment. Cities must strike a balance between mobility and liveability.

ex.t: The expressway was built at the expense of farmland.
ex.vi: Cao tốc được xây bằng cách hy sinh đất nông nghiệp.

ex.t: Owning a car comes at a high cost.
ex.vi: Sở hữu ô tô phải trả giá cao.

ex.t: Drivers pay a toll in exchange for a faster route.
ex.vi: Tài xế trả phí để đổi lấy tuyến đường nhanh hơn.

ex.t: Planners must weigh convenience against pollution.
ex.vi: Nhà quy hoạch phải cân nhắc sự tiện lợi với ô nhiễm.

drill.t: Speed often comes at ___ cost of safety.
drill.vi: Tốc độ thường phải đánh đổi an toàn.

drill.t: We need to strike a balance ___ cars and pedestrians.
drill.vi: Cần cân bằng giữa ô tô và người đi bộ.

drill.vi: Đường mở rộng bằng cách hy sinh công viên.

cue.card: Describe a journey that took much longer than you expected.
points: and explain how you felt about it
model: I’d like to describe a trip from Hanoi to my grandparents’ village in Nam Dinh during the Tết holiday two years ago — a journey that normally takes two hours but ended up taking nearly seven.
My father drove the family car, with my mother, my younger brother and me, plus a boot full of gifts. We set off on the afternoon before New Year’s Eve, which, in hindsight, was a terrible decision.

The main problem was simply volume. It seemed as if the entire population of Hanoi had decided to go home at the same moment. The expressway was gridlocked for kilometres, and when we tried to take a smaller road, we found it equally jammed with motorbikes carrying families, peach trees and boxes of food. A minor accident near a toll gate made things even worse.

At first I was extremely frustrated — I kept checking the map app, which kept adding minutes to our arrival time. But somewhere around the fourth hour, the mood in the car changed. My parents started telling stories about Tết when they were young, travelling on overcrowded buses, and we shared the snacks meant for my grandparents. I still think the trip showed how car-dependent our holidays have become, and next time I’ll suggest the train — but, oddly, it’s one of my favourite family memories.

write.prompt: In many developing cities, the number of private cars is increasing rapidly. What problems does this cause, and what measures can governments take to tackle them?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase; preview
Body 1: problems — congestion, pollution and health, road safety, land use and inequality
Body 2: measures — public transport first, then pricing and parking reform, land-use planning, active travel
Conclusion: sequence and political will
model: As incomes rise in developing countries, millions of families are buying their first cars, which are often regarded as symbols of success. However, the rapid growth in private vehicles is placing enormous strain on cities. This essay will outline the main problems this causes and suggest measures governments can take.

The most visible consequence is congestion. Cities designed for motorbikes and pedestrians simply do not have the road space for large numbers of cars, each of which carries few people while occupying a large area. Gridlock wastes millions of working hours and raises the cost of goods. Rising car use also worsens air pollution, contributing to respiratory illness, and increases greenhouse gas emissions. Furthermore, space allocated to roads and parking often comes at the expense of pavements, parks and housing, while the benefits go mainly to wealthier households who can afford cars.

Governments have several tools at their disposal, but the order in which they use them is crucial. The first priority should be to provide fast, reliable and affordable public transport, such as metro lines and bus rapid transit, linked to convenient last-mile options like bike sharing and safe pavements. Once these alternatives exist, cities can introduce congestion charges, higher parking fees and low-emission zones that discourage unnecessary car journeys, using the revenue to subsidise public transport. In the longer term, transit-oriented planning, which places housing, jobs and services near stations, reduces the need to travel by car at all.

In conclusion, the rapid increase in private cars causes congestion, pollution and an inefficient use of scarce urban space. By investing first in public transport and then pricing car use fairly, governments can strike a balance between people’s desire for mobility and the need for liveable cities.

units.title: Loneliness in modern society
units.goal: Discuss the causes and consequences of loneliness, using “the extent to which” and precise emotional vocabulary.

words.ex: Chronic loneliness affects people of all ages.
words.exVi: Cô đơn kéo dài ảnh hưởng đến mọi lứa tuổi.

words.ex: Many elderly people are socially isolated.
words.exVi: Nhiều người cao tuổi bị cô lập xã hội.

words.ex: I enjoy a little solitude at weekends.
words.exVi: Tôi thích chút thời gian một mình vào cuối tuần.

words.ex: Single-person households are increasing.
words.exVi: Hộ gia đình một người đang tăng.

words.ex: Villages used to be close-knit communities.
words.exVi: Làng xưa là những cộng đồng gắn bó khăng khít.

words.ex: Social connection protects health.
words.exVi: Kết nối xã hội bảo vệ sức khoẻ.

words.ex: Migrants often lose their support network.
words.exVi: Người di cư thường mất mạng lưới hỗ trợ.

words.ex: She had nobody to confide in.
words.exVi: Cô ấy không có ai để tâm sự.

words.ex: Lonely people often withdraw from others.
words.exVi: Người cô đơn thường thu mình khỏi người khác.

words.vi: chương trình kết bạn (cho người cô đơn)
words.ex: Volunteers in a befriending scheme phone older people weekly.
words.exVi: Tình nguyện viên chương trình kết bạn gọi điện cho người già hằng tuần.

words.vi: kê đơn xã hội (giới thiệu hoạt động cộng đồng)
words.ex: Doctors in the UK use social prescribing.
words.exVi: Bác sĩ ở Anh áp dụng kê đơn xã hội.

words.ex: Meaningful conversations matter more than many contacts.
words.exVi: Cuộc trò chuyện có ý nghĩa quan trọng hơn nhiều mối quen biết.

words.ex: Online friendships can be superficial.
words.exVi: Tình bạn trên mạng có thể hời hợt.

words.ex: Young people migrate to cities for work.
words.exVi: Người trẻ di cư lên thành phố làm việc.

words.vi: tổ trống (con cái đã ra ở riêng)
words.ex: My parents struggled with the empty nest.
words.exVi: Bố mẹ tôi khó thích nghi khi con cái đi xa.

words.ex: Co-living spaces offer shared kitchens and events.
words.exVi: Không gian sống chung có bếp chung và sự kiện.

words.vi: chủ động liên lạc, tìm giúp đỡ
words.ex: Don’t hesitate to reach out to friends.
words.exVi: Đừng ngại liên lạc với bạn bè.

words.vi: “nơi thứ ba” (không phải nhà hay chỗ làm)
words.ex: Cafés act as a third place for many young people.
words.exVi: Quán cà phê là “nơi thứ ba” của nhiều người trẻ.

words.ex: Chronic loneliness is detrimental to health.
words.exVi: Cô đơn kéo dài có hại cho sức khoẻ.

words.ex: The degree to which people feel connected varies.
words.exVi: Mức độ con người cảm thấy kết nối rất khác nhau.

lines.t: Do you like spending time alone?
lines.vi: Bạn có thích dành thời gian một mình không?

lines.t: Yes, in moderation. I need some solitude to recharge after a busy week, but there’s a big difference between choosing to be alone and feeling lonely.
lines.vi: Có, ở mức vừa phải. Tôi cần chút thời gian một mình để nạp lại năng lượng sau tuần bận rộn, nhưng chọn ở một mình và cảm thấy cô đơn khác nhau rất xa.

lines.t: Have you ever felt lonely?
lines.vi: Bạn đã từng thấy cô đơn chưa?

lines.t: Definitely — during my first year after moving to Ho Chi Minh City for work. I knew almost nobody, and although I chatted online with old friends every day, it didn’t really replace having someone to have dinner with.
lines.vi: Chắc chắn — năm đầu chuyển vào TP.HCM làm việc. Tôi hầu như không quen ai, và dù ngày nào cũng nhắn tin với bạn cũ, điều đó không thay thế được việc có người ăn tối cùng.

lines.t: What did you do about it?
lines.vi: Bạn đã làm gì?

lines.t: I joined a running club and a volunteer group. It felt awkward at first, but within a few months I had a real sense of belonging.
lines.vi: Tôi tham gia câu lạc bộ chạy bộ và một nhóm tình nguyện. Ban đầu thấy ngượng, nhưng vài tháng sau tôi có cảm giác thuộc về thực sự.

sents.t: In 2023, the World Health Organization declared loneliness a global public health concern and set up a commission to address it.
sents.vi: Năm 2023, Tổ chức Y tế Thế giới tuyên bố cô đơn là mối lo y tế công cộng toàn cầu và lập một uỷ ban để giải quyết.

sents.t: Studies have linked chronic loneliness to higher risks of heart disease, stroke and dementia.
sents.vi: Nghiên cứu liên hệ cô đơn kéo dài với nguy cơ cao hơn về bệnh tim, đột quỵ và sa sút trí tuệ.

sents.t: Contrary to the stereotype, surveys in several countries suggest that young adults report loneliness at least as often as older people.
sents.vi: Trái với định kiến, khảo sát ở nhiều nước cho thấy người trẻ báo cáo cô đơn ít nhất là thường xuyên như người lớn tuổi.

sents.t: The United Kingdom appointed a minister for loneliness in 2018.
sents.vi: Vương quốc Anh bổ nhiệm bộ trưởng phụ trách vấn đề cô đơn năm 2018.

sents.t: Japan followed in 2021, partly in response to rising isolation during the pandemic.
sents.vi: Nhật Bản làm theo năm 2021, một phần để ứng phó với tình trạng cô lập gia tăng trong đại dịch.

q.q: The WHO considers loneliness a public health concern.
Surveys show that only elderly people experience loneliness.
Japan’s minister for loneliness has reduced suicide rates.

gram.title: The extent to which / the degree to which
gram.rule: the extent / degree to which + clause · To what extent … ? · to a large / limited extent
gram.note: These phrases let you discuss how far something is true, which is exactly what “To what extent” questions require: It is unclear the extent to which social media causes loneliness. The degree to which people feel isolated depends on the quality of their relationships. To a large extent, loneliness is a structural problem.

ex.t: The extent to which technology is to blame is debatable.
ex.vi: Công nghệ có lỗi đến mức nào vẫn còn tranh cãi.

ex.t: To a large extent, loneliness reflects how cities are designed.
ex.vi: Ở mức độ lớn, cô đơn phản ánh cách thành phố được thiết kế.

ex.t: The degree to which people feel connected varies widely.
ex.vi: Mức độ con người cảm thấy kết nối rất khác nhau.

ex.t: I agree only to a limited extent.
ex.vi: Tôi chỉ đồng ý ở mức hạn chế.

drill.t: The extent ___ which this is true is unclear.
drill.vi: Điều này đúng đến mức nào vẫn chưa rõ.

drill.t: To a ___ extent, I agree.
drill.vi: Ở mức độ lớn, tôi đồng ý.

drill.t: To what ___ is the internet responsible?
drill.vi: Internet chịu trách nhiệm đến mức nào?

drill.t: The degree to which people ___ lonely depends on many factors.
drill.vi: Mức độ cô đơn của mỗi người phụ thuộc nhiều yếu tố.

lines.t: Why are people lonelier today, despite being more connected than ever?
lines.vi: Vì sao người ta cô đơn hơn dù kết nối hơn bao giờ hết?

lines.t: I think “connected” is the misleading word. We have more contacts but fewer meaningful relationships. Add to that longer working hours, more people living alone and young people migrating far from home, and the traditional networks of extended family and neighbours have weakened considerably.
lines.vi: Tôi nghĩ “kết nối” là từ gây hiểu lầm. Ta có nhiều mối liên lạc hơn nhưng ít mối quan hệ có ý nghĩa hơn. Thêm giờ làm dài hơn, nhiều người sống một mình và người trẻ di cư xa nhà, các mạng lưới truyền thống như đại gia đình và hàng xóm đã yếu đi đáng kể.

lines.t: Is loneliness a personal problem or a social one?
lines.vi: Cô đơn là vấn đề cá nhân hay xã hội?

lines.t: Both, but I’d say to a large extent it’s structural. If a city has no affordable third places, if people commute two hours a day, and if older people live in tower blocks with broken lifts, individual effort can only do so much.
lines.vi: Cả hai, nhưng tôi cho rằng ở mức độ lớn nó mang tính cấu trúc. Nếu thành phố không có “nơi thứ ba” giá phải chăng, nếu người ta đi làm hai tiếng mỗi ngày, và người già sống trong chung cư thang máy hỏng, nỗ lực cá nhân chỉ làm được đến thế.

lines.t: What can governments do about loneliness?
lines.vi: Chính phủ có thể làm gì về cô đơn?

lines.t: Quite a lot, actually: funding community centres and befriending schemes, supporting social prescribing by doctors and designing housing with shared spaces. Reducing the stigma matters too, so that people feel able to reach out.
lines.vi: Khá nhiều: tài trợ nhà văn hoá và chương trình kết bạn, hỗ trợ bác sĩ kê đơn xã hội và thiết kế nhà ở có không gian chung. Giảm kỳ thị cũng quan trọng, để người ta dám chủ động tìm giúp đỡ.

gram2.title: Precise emotional vocabulary: alone, lonely, isolated, solitary
gram2.rule: alone (physical state) · lonely (painful feeling) · isolated (cut off by circumstances) · solitary (by choice or habit)
gram2.note: These words are often confused. Being alone is neutral; feeling lonely is painful; being isolated describes a situation; a solitary activity is done alone, often by choice. Precision here signals a high lexical score.

ex.t: I live alone, but I rarely feel lonely.
ex.vi: Tôi sống một mình nhưng hiếm khi cô đơn.

ex.t: Villagers became isolated after the floods.
ex.vi: Dân làng bị cô lập sau lũ.

ex.t: Reading is a solitary pleasure.
ex.vi: Đọc sách là niềm vui đơn độc.

ex.t: She felt lonely even in a crowded office.
ex.vi: Cô ấy thấy cô đơn ngay cả ở văn phòng đông người.

drill.t: You can feel ___ in a crowd.
drill.vi: Bạn có thể cô đơn giữa đám đông.

drill.t: He prefers ___ hobbies like fishing.
drill.vi: Anh ấy thích sở thích một mình như câu cá.

drill.t: The storm left the island ___.
drill.vi: Cơn bão khiến hòn đảo bị cô lập.

drill.t: I was home ___ all weekend.
drill.vi: Tôi ở nhà một mình cả cuối tuần.

cue.card: Describe a time when you helped someone who was feeling lonely.
points: and explain how you felt about helping them
model: I’d like to talk about an elderly neighbour of mine, Mrs Lan, who lived alone in the flat opposite ours for several years.

Her husband had passed away, and her only son had migrated to Australia, so apart from a weekly video call she spent most days completely by herself. She was quite proud and never complained, but I noticed she would sometimes sit by her door in the evenings just to say hello to anyone passing. Her lift was also often broken, so she rarely left the building — she was genuinely socially isolated.

It started small. I began stopping to chat when I came home from work, and then I offered to carry her shopping up. Later, I taught her how to order groceries on her phone and helped her join a Zalo group for retired people in our district, which organises morning exercise in the park. Eventually she started joining them three times a week.

Helping her made me feel surprisingly good — probably better than it made her feel, at first. But it also made me realise the extent to which loneliness is hidden. She lived three metres from my door, and for over a year I didn’t notice. Since then I’ve made more effort to know my neighbours, and I think if more people did the same, a lot of quiet loneliness could be prevented.

write.prompt: Many people today feel lonely, even though modern technology makes communication easier than ever. What are the causes of this, and what can be done to reduce loneliness?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase the paradox; preview
Body 1: causes — quantity vs quality of contact, changing living patterns (urbanisation, single households, migration), work and commuting, loss of third places, stigma
Body 2: solutions — community spaces and design, social prescribing and befriending, workplace and school initiatives, reducing stigma
Conclusion: loneliness as a social, not just personal, issue
model: It seems paradoxical that loneliness is widespread in an age when people can contact almost anyone instantly. Yet surveys in many countries suggest that a large proportion of adults, including the young, frequently feel lonely. This essay will examine the reasons for this and propose some ways of addressing it.

One important reason is that technology has increased the quantity of contact rather than its quality. Messages and social media likes can create an illusion of connection while replacing the face-to-face interaction that builds deep relationships. Changes in how people live are also significant. Urbanisation and migration have separated many young people from family networks, while single-person households are growing rapidly as people marry later and live longer. Long working hours and commutes leave little time for friendship, and the gradual disappearance of affordable “third places”, such as community halls and local cafés, removes opportunities for casual social contact. Finally, the stigma attached to admitting loneliness discourages people from seeking help.

Addressing loneliness requires recognising that it is, to a large extent, a social problem rather than a purely personal one. Local governments can fund community centres, parks and libraries that bring people together, and planners can design housing with shared spaces and intergenerational schemes that mix students and older residents. Health systems can adopt social prescribing, through which doctors refer patients to clubs, volunteering or befriending schemes rather than relying solely on medication. Employers and universities can also help by creating structured opportunities for newcomers to meet others. At the same time, public campaigns can reduce stigma, encouraging people to reach out before isolation becomes chronic.

In conclusion, loneliness in modern society stems from superficial digital connection, changing living patterns and the loss of shared spaces. Because its causes are largely structural, the most effective solutions involve communities, health services and urban design, not merely individual effort.

units.title: Happiness & well-being
units.goal: Discuss what makes people happy and whether it can be measured, using complex noun groups and stance adverbs.

words.exVi: Việc theo đuổi hạnh phúc có thể khiến người ta lo âu.

words.exVi: Động lực nội tại bền hơn phần thưởng.

lines.t: What makes you happy?
lines.vi: Điều gì khiến bạn hạnh phúc?

lines.t: Mostly small, ordinary things — a long dinner with friends, finishing a difficult piece of work, cycling along the river early on a Sunday. The things I once assumed would make me happy, like a bigger apartment, turned out to matter far less.
lines.vi: Phần lớn là những điều nhỏ bé, bình thường — bữa tối dài với bạn bè, hoàn thành một việc khó, đạp xe dọc sông sáng sớm Chủ nhật. Những thứ tôi từng nghĩ sẽ khiến mình hạnh phúc, như căn hộ lớn hơn, hoá ra lại ít quan trọng hơn nhiều.

lines.t: Were you happier as a child?
lines.vi: Hồi nhỏ bạn có hạnh phúc hơn không?

lines.t: In a simpler way, perhaps. Children live much more in the present, whereas adults spend a lot of time worrying about the future. But I find my happiness now more meaningful, because it comes partly from things I’ve chosen and worked for.
lines.vi: Theo cách đơn giản hơn, có lẽ vậy. Trẻ em sống trong hiện tại nhiều hơn, còn người lớn dành nhiều thời gian lo lắng về tương lai. Nhưng tôi thấy hạnh phúc của mình bây giờ ý nghĩa hơn, vì một phần đến từ những điều mình đã chọn và nỗ lực vì nó.

lines.t: Do you think people in your country are happy?
lines.vi: Bạn có nghĩ người dân nước bạn hạnh phúc không?

lines.t: Surveys suggest moderately so, and I’d say people are remarkably resilient. Family ties are strong, which undeniably helps, but work pressure and social comparison have increased a lot, especially among young urban people.
lines.vi: Khảo sát cho thấy ở mức khá, và tôi cho rằng người dân kiên cường đáng kể. Gắn kết gia đình bền chặt, điều không thể phủ nhận là có ích, nhưng áp lực công việc và so sánh xã hội đã tăng nhiều, nhất là ở người trẻ thành thị.

sents.t: A widely cited 2010 study concluded that emotional well-being stopped rising once annual income reached about 75,000 dollars.
sents.vi: Một nghiên cứu năm 2010 được dẫn nhiều kết luận rằng hạnh phúc cảm xúc ngừng tăng khi thu nhập năm đạt khoảng 75.000 đô la.

sents.t: A larger study published in 2021, however, found that well-being continued to increase with income well beyond that level.
sents.vi: Tuy nhiên, một nghiên cứu lớn hơn công bố năm 2021 cho thấy hạnh phúc tiếp tục tăng theo thu nhập vượt xa mức đó.

sents.t: In 2023, researchers from both teams collaborated and concluded that the plateau applies mainly to the least happy fifth of people.
sents.vi: Năm 2023, các nhà nghiên cứu của cả hai nhóm hợp tác và kết luận rằng hiện tượng chững lại chủ yếu đúng với một phần năm người kém hạnh phúc nhất.

sents.t: For this group, problems such as illness or grief appear to limit what extra income can achieve.
sents.vi: Với nhóm này, những vấn đề như bệnh tật hay mất mát dường như giới hạn những gì thu nhập thêm có thể đạt được.

sents.t: For most people, though, each doubling of income is associated with a similar, modest increase in well-being.
sents.vi: Tuy nhiên với phần lớn mọi người, mỗi lần thu nhập tăng gấp đôi đi kèm mức tăng hạnh phúc tương tự và khiêm tốn.

q.q: The 2021 study supported the idea of a fixed income limit for happiness.
Researchers from the two original teams later worked together.
The 2023 study was conducted entirely in Europe.

gram.title: Complex noun groups
gram.rule: pre-modification (a widely cited study) · post-modification with prepositions (the pursuit of happiness), participles (people living alone), relative and to-clauses (the ability to adapt)
gram.note: Band 8–9 writing packs information into noun groups instead of chains of short clauses. Build them by adding adjectives and adverbs before the noun and phrases after it: the growing body of evidence linking social media use to anxiety. Keep the head noun clear so the verb agrees with it: The number of studies examining this effect HAS increased.

ex.t: A growing body of research links loneliness to poor health.
ex.vi: Ngày càng nhiều nghiên cứu liên hệ cô đơn với sức khoẻ kém.

ex.t: The pursuit of material wealth rarely brings lasting satisfaction.
ex.vi: Việc theo đuổi của cải vật chất hiếm khi mang lại sự hài lòng lâu dài.

ex.t: People living in close-knit communities report higher well-being.
ex.vi: Những người sống trong cộng đồng gắn bó báo cáo mức hạnh phúc cao hơn.

ex.t: The ability to adapt to change is crucial for resilience.
ex.vi: Khả năng thích nghi với thay đổi là then chốt cho sức bật.

lines.t: Should governments try to increase people’s happiness?
lines.vi: Chính phủ có nên cố gắng tăng hạnh phúc của người dân không?

lines.t: Not directly, I’d argue — a government telling citizens how to be happy sounds rather sinister. But it can address the conditions that undermine well-being: insecure jobs, loneliness, poor mental health services, long commutes. Ostensibly economic policies, like housing, often have the biggest effect on how people feel.
lines.vi: Tôi cho là không nên trực tiếp — chính phủ bảo công dân cách để hạnh phúc nghe khá đáng sợ. Nhưng họ có thể giải quyết những điều kiện làm suy giảm hạnh phúc: việc làm bấp bênh, cô đơn, dịch vụ sức khoẻ tinh thần kém, đi lại xa. Những chính sách bề ngoài là kinh tế như nhà ở thường tác động lớn nhất đến cảm nhận của người dân.

lines.t: Is GDP a good measure of a country’s success?
lines.vi: GDP có phải thước đo tốt cho thành công của một quốc gia?

lines.t: It’s a good measure of economic activity, but a poor measure of success. GDP rises after a natural disaster because of rebuilding, and it counts pollution clean-up as growth. Several countries now publish well-being indicators alongside GDP, which seems a sensible complement rather than a replacement.
lines.vi: Đó là thước đo tốt cho hoạt động kinh tế, nhưng là thước đo kém cho thành công. GDP tăng sau thiên tai vì tái thiết, và nó tính việc dọn dẹp ô nhiễm là tăng trưởng. Một số nước giờ công bố chỉ số hạnh phúc song song với GDP, có vẻ là sự bổ sung hợp lý chứ không phải thay thế.

lines.t: Why might richer societies not be happier?
lines.vi: Vì sao xã hội giàu hơn có thể không hạnh phúc hơn?

lines.t: Partly hedonic adaptation — we quickly get used to higher living standards — and partly social comparison: if everyone’s income rises, nobody feels relatively better off. Rich societies can also lose things that are hard to price, like time with family or a sense of community.
lines.vi: Một phần là do thích nghi khoái lạc — ta nhanh chóng quen với mức sống cao hơn — và một phần do so sánh xã hội: nếu thu nhập của ai cũng tăng, không ai cảm thấy khá hơn tương đối. Xã hội giàu cũng có thể đánh mất những thứ khó định giá, như thời gian bên gia đình hay ý thức cộng đồng.

gram2.title: Stance adverbs
gram2.rule: admittedly · arguably · conceivably · ostensibly · undeniably · understandably · paradoxically · predictably
gram2.note: Stance adverbs show your attitude to a statement in a single word, which is elegant and efficient. Each has a precise meaning: ostensibly = it appears so, but may not be true; conceivably = it is possible to imagine; paradoxically = surprisingly contradictory. Place them at the start of a sentence or before the main verb.

ex.t: Paradoxically, the more choices people have, the less satisfied they feel.
ex.vi: Nghịch lý thay, người ta càng có nhiều lựa chọn càng kém hài lòng.

ex.t: The policy was ostensibly designed to help families.
ex.vi: Chính sách bề ngoài được thiết kế để giúp các gia đình.

ex.t: Admittedly, income does matter up to a point.
ex.vi: Phải thừa nhận rằng thu nhập có quan trọng đến một mức nào đó.

ex.t: Understandably, people prioritise security in uncertain times.
ex.vi: Dễ hiểu là người ta ưu tiên sự an toàn trong thời bất ổn.

cue.card: Describe a time when you felt very satisfied with something you achieved.
points: what you had to do to achieve it
and explain why it gave you so much satisfaction
model: The achievement I’d like to describe is completing my first half-marathon, which I ran in Hanoi about two years ago — not quickly, I should say, but without stopping.

What makes it meaningful is where I started from. A year earlier, I was someone who got out of breath climbing the stairs to my office on the fourth floor. After a health check flagged high blood pressure, I decided I needed a concrete goal rather than vague intentions, so I signed up for the race nine months in advance, which made it embarrassing to back out. I followed a beginner’s programme, starting with alternating one minute of jogging and one of walking, and gradually built up to three runs a week. There were plenty of setbacks — a knee injury in the fourth month set me back several weeks — and more than once I seriously considered giving up.

The satisfaction came less from crossing the finish line itself, which was mostly painful, than from what it represented. It was undeniably the first time as an adult that I’d set myself a long-term goal with no external reward — no grade, no salary — and achieved it through steady, unglamorous effort. Paradoxically, the most valuable thing I gained wasn’t fitness but a kind of evidence about myself: that I can change habits I’d assumed were fixed. That has made me more willing to take on other difficult things since.

write.prompt: Some people believe that economic growth is the best way for a country to improve the happiness of its citizens. Others argue that other factors are more important. Discuss both views and give your own opinion.
plan: Introduction: precise paraphrase + nuanced thesis (growth is necessary up to a point but insufficient; distribution and non-material factors dominate in middle/high-income countries)
Body 1: case for growth — poverty, health, security; evidence from income–well-being studies
Body 2: case for other factors — diminishing returns, relative income, relationships, trust, health systems; Nordic/Costa Rica example
Conclusion: synthesis — growth as a means, not an end
model: Whether prosperity is the most reliable route to a happier population is a question that divides economists and policymakers. While some maintain that economic growth remains the most effective means of raising well-being, others contend that factors such as social relationships, health and public trust matter more. In my view, growth is indispensable for poorer nations, but beyond a certain level of income, how wealth is distributed and how people live become considerably more important than further expansion.

The argument for prioritising growth is strongest where material deprivation is widespread. Rising national income allows governments to fund clean water, healthcare and education, and it enables households to escape the chronic insecurity that poverty brings. Large-scale studies consistently find that, within and across countries, richer people report higher life satisfaction on average, and recent research suggests that this association persists even at relatively high incomes. From this perspective, dismissing growth as irrelevant to happiness would be both inaccurate and, for the world’s poorest, irresponsible.

Nevertheless, the relationship between income and well-being is far from straightforward. Each additional dollar tends to produce a smaller gain in happiness than the last, and because people judge their circumstances partly by comparison with others, a general rise in incomes can leave individuals feeling no better off. Moreover, several of the factors most strongly linked to life satisfaction — secure employment, close relationships, good physical and mental health, and trust in public institutions — are only loosely connected to GDP. This helps to explain why countries such as Costa Rica report levels of well-being comparable to those of far wealthier nations, while some rapidly growing economies have seen little improvement in how their citizens feel.

In conclusion, economic growth is a necessary foundation for happiness, particularly in low-income countries, but it is not sufficient on its own. Governments of middle- and high-income countries should therefore treat growth as a means rather than an end, and judge their success by broader measures that capture health, social connection and security, alongside the conventional indicators of prosperity.

units.title: Surveillance & privacy
units.goal: Debate privacy, security and data, using the formal subjunctive and inverted conditionals.

words.ex: Critics warn against becoming a surveillance state.
words.exVi: Những người phê phán cảnh báo về nguy cơ trở thành nhà nước giám sát.

words.ex: A data breach exposed millions of passwords.
words.exVi: Một vụ rò rỉ dữ liệu làm lộ hàng triệu mật khẩu.

words.ex: End-to-end encryption protects messages.
words.exVi: Mã hoá đầu cuối bảo vệ tin nhắn.

words.ex: Online anonymity can protect whistle-blowers.
words.exVi: Ẩn danh trên mạng có thể bảo vệ người tố giác.

words.ex: Almost nobody reads the terms and conditions.
words.exVi: Hầu như không ai đọc điều khoản và điều kiện.

words.ex: Security laws must respect civil liberties.
words.exVi: Luật an ninh phải tôn trọng quyền tự do dân sự.

words.ex: The app is highly intrusive.
words.exVi: Ứng dụng có tính xâm phạm cao.

words.ex: Surveillance must be proportionate to the threat.
words.exVi: Giám sát phải tương xứng với mối đe doạ.

words.ex: An independent oversight body reviews requests.
words.exVi: Một cơ quan giám sát độc lập xem xét các yêu cầu.

words.ex: The whistle-blower revealed illegal monitoring.
words.exVi: Người tố giác đã tiết lộ việc theo dõi trái phép.

words.ex: Metadata reveals who you called and when.
words.exVi: Siêu dữ liệu tiết lộ bạn gọi cho ai và khi nào.

words.vi: lập hồ sơ (dựa trên dữ liệu)
words.ex: Algorithmic profiling can be discriminatory.
words.exVi: Lập hồ sơ bằng thuật toán có thể mang tính phân biệt.

words.ex: EU citizens have the right to be forgotten.
words.exVi: Công dân EU có quyền được lãng quên.

words.ex: Surveillance has a chilling effect on free speech.
words.exVi: Giám sát tạo hiệu ứng khiến người ta ngại tự do ngôn luận.

words.ex: There is a trade-off between privacy and convenience.
words.exVi: Có sự đánh đổi giữa quyền riêng tư và sự tiện lợi.

words.ex: Fingerprints and face scans are biometric data.

words.exVi: Các nền tảng kiếm tiền từ sự chú ý của người dùng.

words.exVi: Người dùng nên có thể dễ dàng chọn không tham gia.

words.exVi: Cảnh sát cần lệnh để khám điện thoại của bạn.

lines.t: Do you worry about your privacy online?
lines.vi: Bạn có lo về quyền riêng tư trên mạng không?

lines.t: More than I used to. I’ve started reading which permissions apps request, and I was genuinely surprised how many want my location or contacts for no obvious reason.
lines.vi: Nhiều hơn trước. Tôi bắt đầu đọc xem ứng dụng xin những quyền gì, và thực sự ngạc nhiên vì nhiều ứng dụng muốn vị trí hay danh bạ của tôi mà không có lý do rõ ràng.

lines.t: Do you share much on social media?
lines.vi: Bạn có chia sẻ nhiều trên mạng xã hội không?

lines.t: Very little now. I post occasionally, but never anything that reveals where I live or my daily routine. A friend had her account hacked a few years ago and it made me much more cautious.
lines.vi: Giờ rất ít. Thỉnh thoảng tôi đăng bài, nhưng không bao giờ đăng gì tiết lộ nơi ở hay lịch sinh hoạt. Một người bạn bị hack tài khoản vài năm trước và điều đó khiến tôi thận trọng hơn nhiều.

lines.t: Is privacy more important to older or younger people?
lines.vi: Quyền riêng tư quan trọng với người lớn tuổi hay người trẻ hơn?

lines.t: Younger people share more, but research suggests they care about privacy just as much — they just manage it differently, for instance by using private accounts or messaging apps instead of public posts.
lines.vi: Người trẻ chia sẻ nhiều hơn, nhưng nghiên cứu cho thấy họ quan tâm đến quyền riêng tư không kém — chỉ là quản lý khác đi, chẳng hạn dùng tài khoản riêng tư hay ứng dụng nhắn tin thay vì đăng công khai.

sents.t: Governments sometimes argue that collecting metadata is harmless because it does not include the content of communications.
sents.vi: Các chính phủ đôi khi cho rằng thu thập siêu dữ liệu là vô hại vì nó không bao gồm nội dung liên lạc.

sents.t: However, a study at Stanford University showed that phone metadata alone could reveal sensitive information about people’s lives.
sents.vi: Tuy nhiên, một nghiên cứu ở Đại học Stanford cho thấy chỉ riêng siêu dữ liệu điện thoại có thể tiết lộ thông tin nhạy cảm về cuộc sống con người.

sents.t: From the times and numbers of calls, researchers could infer that participants had medical conditions or had visited certain clinics.
sents.vi: Từ thời điểm và số điện thoại của các cuộc gọi, các nhà nghiên cứu có thể suy ra người tham gia mắc bệnh hay đã đến một số phòng khám.

sents.t: The researchers emphasised that this required no special technology, only careful analysis.
sents.vi: Các nhà nghiên cứu nhấn mạnh rằng điều này không cần công nghệ đặc biệt, chỉ cần phân tích cẩn thận.

sents.t: Their findings have been cited in legal challenges to mass data collection.
sents.vi: Kết quả của họ đã được dẫn chứng trong các vụ kiện phản đối việc thu thập dữ liệu hàng loạt.

q.q: Metadata includes the content of phone conversations.
The researchers did not need specialised technology.
The study led to a ban on metadata collection in the US.

gram.title: The formal subjunctive
gram.rule: recommend / insist / demand / propose / require + that + subject + base verb · It is essential / vital / imperative that + subject + base verb (be, have, not do)
gram.note: After verbs and adjectives of necessity or recommendation, formal English uses the base form of the verb for every subject, including he, she and it: The committee recommended that the law be reviewed. Negative: that he not be informed. British English often uses should instead (that the law should be reviewed), which is also correct.

ex.t: Campaigners demanded that the database be deleted.
ex.vi: Các nhà vận động đòi xoá bỏ cơ sở dữ liệu.

ex.t: It is essential that every request be approved by a judge.
ex.vi: Điều thiết yếu là mọi yêu cầu phải được thẩm phán phê duyệt.

ex.t: The report recommends that users be told how their data is used.
ex.vi: Báo cáo khuyến nghị người dùng phải được thông báo cách dữ liệu của họ được sử dụng.

ex.t: The law requires that companies not sell data without consent.
ex.vi: Luật yêu cầu công ty không được bán dữ liệu khi chưa có sự đồng ý.

drill.vi: Họ yêu cầu cô ấy phải có mặt.

drill.t: It is vital that the system ___ secure.
drill.vi: Điều tối quan trọng là hệ thống phải an toàn.

drill.t: The judge ordered that the data ___ destroyed.
drill.vi: Thẩm phán ra lệnh huỷ dữ liệu.

drill.t: I propose that he ___ given access.
drill.vi: Tôi đề nghị không cấp quyền truy cập cho anh ấy.

lines.t: Is it acceptable for governments to monitor citizens to prevent crime?
lines.vi: Chính phủ giám sát công dân để ngăn tội phạm có chấp nhận được không?

lines.t: Targeted monitoring, with a warrant and independent oversight, seems reasonable — that’s how police investigations have always worked. Mass surveillance of everyone is different. It treats the entire population as suspects, and history suggests that powers introduced for one purpose tend to expand to others.
lines.vi: Giám sát có mục tiêu, có lệnh và giám sát độc lập, có vẻ hợp lý — điều tra của cảnh sát vốn hoạt động như vậy. Giám sát hàng loạt mọi người thì khác. Nó coi toàn bộ dân chúng là nghi phạm, và lịch sử cho thấy quyền lực được tạo ra cho một mục đích thường mở rộng sang mục đích khác.

lines.t: What do you think of the argument “If you have nothing to hide, you have nothing to fear”?
lines.vi: Bạn nghĩ gì về lập luận “Không có gì để giấu thì không có gì phải sợ”?

lines.t: I think it misunderstands what privacy is for. Everyone has things that are legal but private — medical issues, financial problems, relationships. And what counts as “wrong” depends on who’s in power; information that’s harmless today could be used against people under a different government.
lines.vi: Tôi nghĩ nó hiểu sai mục đích của quyền riêng tư. Ai cũng có những điều hợp pháp nhưng riêng tư — sức khoẻ, tài chính, các mối quan hệ. Và điều gì bị coi là “sai” phụ thuộc vào ai đang nắm quyền; thông tin vô hại hôm nay có thể bị dùng chống lại người dân dưới một chính quyền khác.

lines.t: Are companies a bigger threat to privacy than governments?
lines.vi: Doanh nghiệp có phải mối đe doạ lớn hơn chính phủ đối với quyền riêng tư không?

lines.t: In everyday terms, possibly, because they collect far more detailed data and their business model depends on monetising it. But governments have powers companies don’t — they can arrest you. So the most worrying situation is when the two combine, with authorities able to access corporate data without proper safeguards.
lines.vi: Xét đời thường thì có thể, vì họ thu thập dữ liệu chi tiết hơn nhiều và mô hình kinh doanh dựa trên việc kiếm tiền từ nó. Nhưng chính phủ có quyền lực mà doanh nghiệp không có — họ có thể bắt giữ bạn. Nên tình huống đáng lo nhất là khi hai bên kết hợp, cơ quan chức năng có thể truy cập dữ liệu doanh nghiệp mà không có biện pháp bảo vệ phù hợp.

gram2.title: Inverted conditionals
gram2.rule: Should + subject + verb (= If … should) · Were + subject + to + verb (= If … were to) · Had + subject + past participle (= If … had)
gram2.note: In formal writing, you can omit if and invert the subject and auxiliary. Should you require assistance… is a polite formal condition. Were governments to ban encryption, … describes a hypothetical future. Had the data been encrypted, the breach would not have occurred refers to the past. These are rare and impressive — use one at most per essay.

ex.t: Should a breach occur, users must be informed immediately.
ex.vi: Nếu xảy ra rò rỉ, người dùng phải được thông báo ngay.

ex.t: Were encryption to be banned, criminals would simply use illegal tools.
ex.vi: Nếu mã hoá bị cấm, tội phạm sẽ đơn giản dùng công cụ bất hợp pháp.

ex.t: Had the company encrypted its files, the leak would have been harmless.
ex.vi: Nếu công ty mã hoá tệp, vụ rò rỉ đã vô hại.

ex.t: Should you have any questions, please contact us.
ex.vi: Nếu có câu hỏi, xin vui lòng liên hệ chúng tôi.

drill.t: ___ the police need access, they must obtain a warrant.
drill.vi: Nếu cảnh sát cần truy cập, họ phải có lệnh.

drill.t: ___ I known, I would have deleted it.
drill.vi: Nếu tôi biết, tôi đã xoá nó.

drill.t: Were the law ___, privacy would suffer.
drill.vi: Nếu luật thay đổi, quyền riêng tư sẽ bị ảnh hưởng.

drill.t: ___ it not for the leak, nobody would know.
drill.vi: Nếu không có vụ rò rỉ, sẽ chẳng ai biết.

cue.card: Describe a time when you were concerned about your personal information being shared.
points: how it was shared or might have been shared
and explain how you felt about the situation
model: I’d like to talk about an incident about three years ago, when I received a phone call from someone claiming to be from my bank. The caller knew my full name, my address, the last four digits of my card and — this was the unsettling part — the name of the insurance product I had bought a few weeks earlier.

They said there had been suspicious activity on my account and asked me to confirm a code that had just been sent to my phone. Fortunately, something about the urgency of their tone made me hesitate, so I said I’d call the bank back myself. When I did, the bank confirmed it was a scam, and that the code would have allowed the caller to authorise a transfer. What I never found out was how they had obtained such specific details. The most likely explanation, the bank suggested, was a data breach at a third party — perhaps the insurance company or one of its agents.

I froze my card, changed all my passwords and filed a complaint, but I never received a clear explanation from either company, which was frustrating. I think what affected me most was the feeling of being exposed without having done anything careless. It made the abstract idea of a “data breach” very concrete. Since then I’ve been far more reluctant to give personal details to businesses, and I’m convinced that it is essential that companies be legally required to tell customers when their data has been compromised.

write.prompt: Many governments now use technology such as facial recognition cameras in public places to improve security. Do the advantages of this outweigh the disadvantages?
plan: Introduction: paraphrase + clear answer (disadvantages outweigh for mass deployment; targeted, regulated use acceptable)
Body 1: advantages — crime detection, missing persons, deterrence; fair, specific
Body 2: disadvantages — error rates and bias, chilling effect, function creep, data security; evidence
Conclusion: answer + conditions (legislation, warrants, independent oversight, transparency)
model: The use of facial recognition cameras in streets, stations and other public spaces has expanded rapidly as governments seek new ways to enhance security. Although this technology offers genuine benefits for law enforcement, I believe that, in its current form of widespread and loosely regulated deployment, its disadvantages outweigh its advantages.

Supporters of facial recognition point to several clear benefits. The technology can identify suspects far more quickly than human officers reviewing hours of footage, and it has helped police locate missing children and vulnerable adults within minutes rather than days. Its visible presence may also deter some crimes, such as theft and violence in crowded transport hubs. For citizens who feel unsafe in public spaces, these are not trivial gains, and it would be unrealistic to expect authorities to ignore a tool that can make investigations considerably more efficient.

However, these advantages come at a substantial cost. Independent testing has shown that some systems are markedly less accurate for women and people with darker skin, so errors are not randomly distributed but fall disproportionately on certain groups, potentially leading to wrongful stops or arrests. More fundamentally, constant identification in public spaces alters the relationship between citizens and the state. When people know that their every movement can be recorded, they may avoid lawful protests or sensitive locations, such as clinics or places of worship — a chilling effect that weakens civil liberties. There is also the risk of function creep: databases created to catch serious criminals may gradually be used for minor offences or political monitoring, and any centralised store of biometric data is an attractive target for hackers.

In conclusion, while facial recognition can make policing more effective, the risks of discrimination, the erosion of freedom and the misuse of data outweigh these benefits when the technology is deployed on a mass scale. Were it to be used at all, it is essential that its use be restricted to serious crimes, authorised by a judge in each case and subject to independent oversight and full public transparency.

units.title: Free speech & online platforms
units.goal: Discuss the limits of free expression and platform responsibility, using argumentative discourse markers and precise reporting.

words.ex: Freedom of expression is a fundamental right.
words.exVi: Tự do ngôn luận là quyền cơ bản.

words.ex: Hate speech targets people for their identity.
words.exVi: Ngôn từ thù ghét nhắm vào con người vì bản sắc của họ.

words.vi: kiểm duyệt nội dung (của nền tảng)
words.ex: Content moderation is done partly by AI.
words.exVi: Kiểm duyệt nội dung một phần do AI thực hiện.

words.ex: The post incited violence.
words.exVi: Bài đăng kích động bạo lực.

words.ex: She sued the newspaper for defamation.
words.exVi: Cô ấy kiện tờ báo tội phỉ báng.

words.ex: Platforms profit from engagement.
words.exVi: Các nền tảng kiếm lời từ tương tác.

words.ex: Algorithms amplify outrage.
words.exVi: Thuật toán khuếch đại sự phẫn nộ.

words.vi: gỡ khỏi nền tảng, cấm tài khoản
words.ex: The influencer was de-platformed after repeated violations.
words.exVi: Người có ảnh hưởng bị cấm tài khoản sau nhiều lần vi phạm.

words.ex: Fear of abuse leads to self-censorship.
words.exVi: Nỗi sợ bị công kích dẫn đến tự kiểm duyệt.

words.ex: In a marketplace of ideas, good arguments should win.
words.exVi: Trong thị trường ý tưởng, lập luận tốt sẽ thắng.

words.ex: Political polarisation has increased.
words.exVi: Sự phân cực chính trị đã gia tăng.

words.ex: Granted, some content is harmful.
words.exVi: Phải công nhận rằng một số nội dung có hại.

words.ex: Conversely, too little moderation allows abuse.
words.exVi: Ngược lại, kiểm duyệt quá ít cho phép lạm dụng.

words.vi: tương tự như vậy, cùng lý lẽ đó
words.ex: By the same token, governments must not abuse these laws.
words.exVi: Tương tự như vậy, chính phủ không được lạm dụng các luật này.

words.ex: The minister refuted the allegations.
words.exVi: Bộ trưởng bác bỏ các cáo buộc.

words.ex: It is alleged that the account spread false claims.
words.exVi: Có cáo buộc rằng tài khoản lan truyền thông tin sai.

words.ex: The company conceded that mistakes were made.
words.exVi: Công ty thừa nhận đã có sai sót.

words.ex: Critics dismissed the plan as unworkable.
words.exVi: Những người phản đối gạt bỏ kế hoạch là không khả thi.

words.ex: Online regulation is a contentious issue.
words.exVi: Quản lý không gian mạng là vấn đề gây tranh cãi.

words.vi: thủ tục tố tụng hợp pháp
words.ex: Removing content should follow due process.
words.exVi: Gỡ nội dung nên tuân theo quy trình hợp pháp.

lines.t: Do you comment on posts online?
lines.vi: Bạn có bình luận các bài đăng trên mạng không?

lines.t: Rarely. I’ll comment on friends’ posts, but I avoid public discussions about politics or social issues. They tend to become hostile very quickly, and I’ve seen people receive abuse for fairly moderate opinions.
lines.vi: Hiếm khi. Tôi bình luận bài của bạn bè, nhưng tránh thảo luận công khai về chính trị hay vấn đề xã hội. Chúng thường trở nên gay gắt rất nhanh, và tôi từng thấy người ta bị công kích vì những ý kiến khá ôn hoà.

lines.t: Have you ever reported a post?
lines.vi: Bạn đã bao giờ báo cáo một bài đăng chưa?

lines.t: A few times, mostly obvious scams or posts that were clearly abusive. Honestly, I’m never sure whether anyone actually reviews them.
lines.vi: Vài lần, chủ yếu là lừa đảo rõ ràng hoặc bài đăng mang tính xúc phạm rõ ràng. Thật lòng, tôi không bao giờ chắc có ai thực sự xem xét chúng không.

lines.t: Would you like to spend less time online?
lines.vi: Bạn có muốn dành ít thời gian trên mạng hơn không?

lines.t: Definitely. I’ve deleted a couple of apps from my phone, which helped, but I still check messages far more than I need to.
lines.vi: Chắc chắn. Tôi đã xoá vài ứng dụng khỏi điện thoại, điều đó có ích, nhưng tôi vẫn kiểm tra tin nhắn nhiều hơn mức cần thiết.

sents.t: Large social media platforms remove millions of posts every month for breaking their rules.
sents.vi: Các nền tảng mạng xã hội lớn gỡ hàng triệu bài đăng mỗi tháng vì vi phạm quy định.

sents.t: Most of these decisions are made automatically by software, with human reviewers handling only a small proportion.
sents.vi: Phần lớn quyết định này do phần mềm tự động đưa ra, người kiểm duyệt chỉ xử lý một tỉ lệ nhỏ.

sents.t: In 2022, the European Union passed a law requiring large platforms to explain their decisions and allow users to appeal.
sents.vi: Năm 2022, Liên minh châu Âu thông qua luật yêu cầu các nền tảng lớn giải thích quyết định và cho phép người dùng khiếu nại.

sents.t: Supporters say this introduces a degree of due process to what was previously an opaque system.
sents.vi: Những người ủng hộ nói điều này đưa một mức độ thủ tục hợp pháp vào một hệ thống trước đây thiếu minh bạch.

sents.t: Critics worry that heavy fines may encourage companies to remove lawful content simply to avoid risk.
sents.vi: Những người phản đối lo rằng mức phạt nặng có thể khiến công ty gỡ cả nội dung hợp pháp chỉ để tránh rủi ro.

q.q: Human reviewers make most moderation decisions.
The EU law gives users the right to appeal decisions.
The EU law has reduced hate speech by half.

gram.title: Discourse markers for argument
gram.rule: Granted, … · That said, … · By the same token, … · Conversely, … · Even so, … · Be that as it may, … · To put it another way, …
gram.note: Discourse markers guide the reader through complex reasoning. Granted introduces a concession; that said and even so return to your main point; by the same token applies the same logic to another case; conversely introduces the opposite situation. At band 8+, they should feel natural and purposeful — never begin every sentence with one.

ex.t: Granted, some speech causes real harm.
ex.vi: Phải công nhận, một số phát ngôn gây hại thật sự.

ex.t: That said, governments should not decide what is true.
ex.vi: Dù vậy, chính phủ không nên quyết định điều gì là đúng.

ex.t: By the same token, platforms should not silence critics.
ex.vi: Tương tự, các nền tảng không nên bịt miệng người phê bình.

ex.t: Conversely, weak moderation leaves users exposed to abuse.
ex.vi: Ngược lại, kiểm duyệt yếu khiến người dùng dễ bị lạm dụng.

drill.t: ___, the law is imperfect. Even so, it is an improvement.
drill.vi: Phải công nhận luật chưa hoàn hảo. Dù vậy, nó là một bước tiến.

drill.t: Strict rules silence people. ___, no rules allow abuse.
drill.vi: Quy định khắt khe bịt miệng người ta. Ngược lại, không có quy định cho phép lạm dụng.

drill.t: Some posts are harmful. ___, most are not.
drill.vi: Một số bài có hại. Dù vậy, phần lớn thì không.

drill.t: If users must follow rules, ___, so must platforms.
drill.vi: Nếu người dùng phải theo quy tắc thì tương tự, nền tảng cũng vậy.

lines.t: Should there be any limits on free speech?
lines.vi: Có nên có giới hạn nào cho tự do ngôn luận không?

lines.t: Some, yes, and almost every legal system already has them — you can’t incite violence or defame someone. The difficulty is drawing the line. Speech that offends people shouldn’t be banned, because that would give authorities enormous power to silence criticism; speech that directly endangers people is different.
lines.vi: Có một vài, và gần như mọi hệ thống pháp luật đều đã có — bạn không thể kích động bạo lực hay phỉ báng ai đó. Cái khó là vạch ranh giới. Phát ngôn gây khó chịu không nên bị cấm, vì như vậy sẽ trao cho chính quyền quyền lực khổng lồ để bịt miệng phê bình; phát ngôn trực tiếp gây nguy hiểm cho con người thì khác.

lines.t: Should social media companies be responsible for what users post?
lines.vi: Công ty mạng xã hội có nên chịu trách nhiệm cho những gì người dùng đăng?

lines.t: Not in the way a newspaper is for its articles — the volume is simply too great. But they should be responsible for what they actively amplify. If an algorithm deliberately pushes inflammatory content to millions because it increases engagement, that’s a decision the company has made.
lines.vi: Không theo cách một tờ báo chịu trách nhiệm cho bài viết của mình — khối lượng đơn giản là quá lớn. Nhưng họ nên chịu trách nhiệm cho những gì họ chủ động khuếch đại. Nếu thuật toán cố tình đẩy nội dung kích động đến hàng triệu người vì nó tăng tương tác, đó là quyết định của công ty.

lines.t: Has the internet been good or bad for public debate?
lines.vi: Internet tốt hay xấu cho tranh luận công cộng?

lines.t: Both, paradoxically. It has given a voice to people who were previously excluded, which is a huge democratic gain. Conversely, it rewards outrage and certainty over nuance, which pushes debates towards polarisation and makes compromise harder.
lines.vi: Nghịch lý là cả hai. Nó trao tiếng nói cho những người trước đây bị loại trừ, một thành quả dân chủ lớn. Ngược lại, nó thưởng cho sự phẫn nộ và chắc chắn hơn là sắc thái, đẩy tranh luận về phía phân cực và khiến thoả hiệp khó hơn.

gram2.title: Precise reporting verbs for claims
gram2.rule: allege (unproven accusation) · refute (prove wrong) · deny (say it is not true) · concede (admit reluctantly) · dismiss (reject as unimportant) · maintain (keep insisting)
gram2.note: Choosing the exact reporting verb shows the reader the status of a claim. Refute means you prove a claim false — it is stronger than deny or reject. Allege is used for accusations not yet proved. Concede signals a reluctant admission. Using these accurately is a mark of very high Lexical Resource.

ex.t: The company denied that it had sold user data.
ex.vi: Công ty phủ nhận đã bán dữ liệu người dùng.

ex.t: Researchers refuted the claim with new evidence.
ex.vi: Các nhà nghiên cứu bác bỏ khẳng định bằng bằng chứng mới.

ex.t: The platform conceded that its system had failed.
ex.vi: Nền tảng thừa nhận hệ thống của họ đã thất bại.

ex.t: Critics dismissed the policy as a publicity stunt.
ex.vi: Những người phản đối gạt bỏ chính sách như một chiêu trò quảng cáo.

drill.t: He ___ the accusation, but offered no proof.
drill.vi: Anh ta phủ nhận cáo buộc nhưng không đưa ra bằng chứng.

drill.t: The study ___ the myth with clear data.
drill.vi: Nghiên cứu bác bỏ hoang đường bằng dữ liệu rõ ràng.

drill.t: It is ___ that the account was fake.
drill.vi: Có cáo buộc rằng tài khoản là giả.

drill.t: She finally ___ that she had been wrong.
drill.vi: Cuối cùng cô ấy thừa nhận mình đã sai.

cue.card: Describe a discussion or debate you took part in where people had different opinions.
points: and explain how the discussion ended and what you learned
model: I’d like to describe a debate in our family group chat last year, which spilled over into a rather tense Sunday lunch. The topic was whether my teenage cousin, who is fifteen, should be allowed to use social media at all.

My aunt, her mother, had just read an article about the effects of social media on teenage girls’ mental health and wanted to ban it completely until she was eighteen. My uncle thought that was unrealistic, since all her classmates communicate through these apps and she would effectively be excluded. My grandmother, rather unexpectedly, sided with my aunt, saying that young people had become “unable to look at each other”. And my cousin, understandably, argued that she was being punished for something she hadn’t done.

For a while it was quite heated, and I mostly listened. Eventually someone — I think it was my uncle — conceded that the research my aunt cited was worrying, and my aunt, for her part, admitted that a total ban might simply push my cousin to use accounts secretly. So they agreed on a compromise: no phone in the bedroom at night, no public profile, and a monthly conversation about anything that had upset her online. What I learned was that the most productive moment came when people stopped arguing about who was right and started discussing what each side was actually afraid of. Granted, it was only a family argument, but I think the same is true of much larger public debates.

write.prompt: The table shows the number of pieces of content removed by a social media platform in 2022 and 2024, by reason, and the percentage detected automatically before any user reported it. Summarise the information by selecting and reporting the main features, and make comparisons where relevant.
write.data:
Reason                 Removed 2022 (millions)   Removed 2024 (millions)   Auto-detected 2022   Auto-detected 2024
Spam                   1,200                    1,850                     99%                  99%
Fake accounts            640                      910                     97%                  99%
Hate speech               22                       15                     82%                  95%
Violent content           35                       41                     93%                  98%
Harassment                 9                       11                     28%                  47%
plan: Introduction: paraphrase both measures
Overview: spam and fake accounts dominate volumes and rose; hate speech the only fall; automation rose across categories but harassment remains far less automated
Body 1: volumes — scale difference, increases; hate speech decline
Body 2: detection — near-total automation for spam/fake; big gains in hate speech; harassment lowest despite rising
model: The table compares the quantity of content that a social media platform removed in 2022 and 2024 for five different reasons, together with the proportion of that content which was identified automatically before being reported by users.

Overall, spam and fake accounts accounted for the overwhelming majority of removals in both years, and both categories grew substantially. Hate speech was the only category to decline. Meanwhile, the share of content detected automatically rose in every category except spam, where it was already almost complete, although harassment remained far less likely to be identified by the platform’s systems than any other type.

In terms of volume, spam removals increased by around half, from 1.2 billion to 1.85 billion, while the number of fake accounts taken down rose from 640 million to 910 million. The remaining categories involved far smaller numbers. Removals of violent content and harassment grew slightly, to 41 million and 11 million respectively, whereas those relating to hate speech fell from 22 million to 15 million.

Automated detection was virtually total for spam and fake accounts, at 97–99%, and it also improved for violent content, reaching 98%. The most notable progress was in hate speech, where the proportion detected automatically climbed from 82% to 95%. Harassment, by contrast, remained the clear exception: although automatic detection rose from just over a quarter to 47%, more than half of such content was still removed only after users had reported it.

units.title: Longevity & the science of ageing
units.goal: Speculate about longer lives and their consequences, using structures for future likelihood and risk collocations.

words.ex: Genes explain only part of longevity.
words.exVi: Gen chỉ giải thích một phần tuổi thọ.

words.ex: Untested treatments pose a risk to patients.
words.exVi: Liệu pháp chưa thử nghiệm gây rủi ro cho bệnh nhân.

words.ex: Only the rich may reap the benefits.

words.ex: Longer lives raise questions of intergenerational fairness.
words.exVi: Sống lâu hơn đặt ra câu hỏi về công bằng giữa các thế hệ.

words.ex: The pension age is rising to 68.
words.exVi: Tuổi hưởng lương hưu đang tăng lên 68.

words.ex: Exercise reduces frailty in later life.
words.exVi: Tập luyện giảm sự yếu ớt khi về già.

words.ex: Biomarkers can show biological age.
words.exVi: Dấu ấn sinh học có thể cho thấy tuổi sinh học.

words.ex: Claims about living to 150 are speculative.
words.exVi: Tuyên bố sống đến 150 tuổi mang tính suy đoán.

words.ex: Services for the elderly need more funding.
words.exVi: Dịch vụ cho người cao tuổi cần thêm kinh phí.
